description: A user signs up, logs back in, and reads their own data with the session they were handed. The same spec then drives ADR 0008 across the seam: a licence key is a giftable bearer claim that unlocks exactly one active account. The lane's Gumroad stub keys the sale on the licence key, so a second signup presenting the same key under another email is refused with the generic invalid_license and never learns the key was valid; deleting the first account through DELETE /users/me erases the binding (the receipt names licensebinding) and one new account then redeems the same key, inheriting access and nothing else; a third attempt is refused again. Backend suites prove the atomicity and the byte-identical refusals with an in-process client; this is the one place the production client, the Postgres UNIQUE constraint on gumroad_sale_id and the deletion cascade are exercised together. One journey rather than two because the ledger lets a spec cover exactly one journey.

A user who cannot log in asks for a reset from ForgotPasswordScreen, reads the email that arrives, follows the https link a browser can actually open, sets a new password on ResetPasswordScreen, and logs in with it; the "this wasn't me" arm cancels the token instead. This is the journey the outage came through: reset mail went to a production log for one reason and carried nothing but an adepthood:// deep link for another, and the endpoint answered 202 through both while every backend suite stayed green. The spec reads the plaintext token out of the rendered body and out of nowhere else, anchored on the https origin APP_BASE_URL configured, so a body that offered only the deep link fails it. The lane reaches that body by booting the server with EMAIL_BACKEND=capture, an adapter that appends every rendered message verbatim to a file and refuses to be built at all when ENV names production. The client-side required-field guard added for #2822 deliberately stops short of this seam: a blank or whitespace-only Send Reset Link now returns before the API client is called, so there is no request for a spec here to observe and the rate-limit budget this route spends per hour is never touched. That behaviour is pinned in the Jest suite for ForgotPasswordScreen; this journey is unchanged by it and stays covered.

A user logs in and is handed a session that lives thirty days rather than an hour (#2804); a refresh rotates it, the rotated token reads their data, and the token rotated away is refused on the very next call even though its exp is weeks out. The backend suite asserts the minted lifetime and the revocation row in-process; this is the place the production client's refresh call, the jti revocation `/auth/refresh` writes, and the lookup every authenticated route performs are exercised together across the wire. The half-life renewal the client schedules against that lifetime is a timer, so it stays in the Jest suite for AuthContext.

A signed-out reader sees the editorial auth layout vertically centred when it fits, then can reach both ends of the Get Started content when the available height shrinks to a keyboard-sized viewport. Every auth route -- Get Started, Login, Signup, Forgot Password, Reset Password and Cancel Reset -- exposes the same scroll surface, and the journey finishes by creating an account through the production client so the tested surface crosses its real seam. The browser half pins actual overflow and centring geometry; the native PR evidence separately exercises iOS 18.6 at accessibility-extra-extra-extra-large because a browser cannot emulate iOS Dynamic Type.

A user taps Continue with Google and the sign-in fails on Google's side: Google refuses the redirect (a misconfigured client, a server error, a state mismatch), or on native the one-time code cannot be traded for an ID token (a refused trade or a dead network). The Google error slot then shows "Google couldn't complete that sign-in. Try again, or continue with email instead." and the button is free to retry, while a user who cancels, dismisses or declines on Google's own screen sees nothing. Uncovered because Playwright cannot drive Google's consent sheet, and every failure leg is produced inside expo-auth-session or Google's token endpoint before any request crosses our seam; pinned meanwhile by useGoogleAuth.test.tsx and the SocialAuthButtons tests.

A new account meets the intro walkthrough, pages through it, and Begin -- or Skip -- hands them to the Journal shelf, which loads the entries they do not have yet. Uncovered because this lane runs on the node environment with node_modules untransformed and cannot mount a screen at all, the same constraint recorded on errors.boundary-recovers-and-reports. The walkthrough's dismissal is a local flag rather than a request, so the only seam a spec here could watch is the shelf's own fetch, which cannot tell that the arrival came from Begin. Covering it needs a second, rendering lane, not another spec here.

A user first tries to create a habit whose name contains only whitespace, a NUL, zero-width text, and Unicode default-ignorables; the production client receives the stable habit_name_empty refusal, and a fresh list proves neither the habit nor its three default goals exists. A visible name wrapped in outer whitespace and a zero-width suffix is then canonicalized on the server and returned without losing its supported Unicode. The user logs 10 units under one tier with a durable operation key; replaying that exact act leaves the server at 10. Logging 5 under the next tier produces a habit-day total of 15, a signed -8 correction crosses the tier boundary to 7, and an oversized -99 correction clamps the entire habit day to 0. A final +10 leaves the freshly listed server state and streak intact. The same client reconciliation that drives the tile is pinned in habitManager.test.ts: it replaces every optimistic row for the affected day with the response's day_units, so reopen and the immediate tile agree.

A user opens a habit modal and leaves the operation on + to add the entered amount, taps once for set to make the selected day's total exact, or taps again for − to subtract the entered amount. Log Units remains the only commit action. The set operation derives the signed correction from that selected calendar day's existing completions before using the ordinary append-only completion route. Uncovered because the browser habit journey logs through its API-backed seam but does not yet open GoalModal; pinned meanwhile by GoalModal.test.tsx for the operation cycle, add/subtract qualification, exact higher and lower totals, selected past-day bucketing, and reset after commit.

A user opens a habit's goal editor, changes its cadence to three times per week, explicitly saves the number, and sees every tier restated in plain language. The same commit is available from Return and blur on web, iOS and Android, with the overlapping native events collapsed into one batch PUT. Uncovered because the current habits browser journey creates and checks in a habit but never opens GoalModal or changes the shared three-tier units; #2814 tracks the seam-crossing epic coverage. Pinned meanwhile by GoalModal.test.tsx for the Save/Return/blur event matrix, invalid and unchanged drafts, shared tooltip/tier copy, GoalModal.starLongPress.test.tsx for the drag-confirm copy and the long-press-fill arbitration, and — after #2884 — GoalModal.markerDrag.test.tsx for the value a marker drop actually saves, backed by markerDrag.test.ts for the drag geometry and HabitUtils.test.ts for the percent-to-target inverse. The drag writes PUT /goals/{goal_id} through the goals client, a different seam from the units batch PUT this journey's editor half uses; both are still mocked in the component lane, which is what 2814 tracks.

A user creates a subtractive habit that began today and has not logged the behavior. The server classifies the three-goal habit by the shared any-goal polarity rule and reports a one-day abstention streak; after a real reload, the Habits tile shows 1 DAYS — ACHIEVED TODAY!, because zero behavior is both a no-log streak day and within the clear ceiling. The browser runs in the user's America/Los_Angeles timezone, so the create/load round-trip also exercises the local calendar boundary rather than reparsing the server's date as UTC midnight.

A regular program habit appears when the program's invitation reaches it. A habit sitting on one of the ten rings waits for that ring to open -- its stage entering the range the calendar and the record between them have unlocked -- and a start date already in the past does not stand in for that (issue #2765: on an established account every start date is past, which opened every ring at once and stopped graduated unlock from tracking the user's level). A habit whose stage names no ring has no rung to wait for, so its start date is still its whole schedule. The habits list read persists the invitation as revealed exactly once; if the person then re-locks it, another read respects the decline instead of re-opening it. The server owns eligibility and its private marker, while the client renders only the reconciled revealed flag. Carryover habits and unrecommitted Metta Return releases remain outside this automatic path, and rows stamped before the stage gate was corrected are left open rather than retroactively re-locked, all pinned by the backend API suite.

A newly registered person whose live habits request succeeds with an empty collection sees an honest first-use state with an Add a habit action, never the fictional names, streaks, or completion history reserved for an explicitly configured demo build. The real-wire spec proves the fresh account and production client receive an empty Page; habitManager.test.ts pins that the service preserves the empty list, and HabitsEmptyState.test.tsx pins the rendered CTA.

A check-in tapped while the device is offline is queued on the device, and the next habits load replays that queue: an entry the server will never accept is dropped so the queue keeps draining behind it, while a dropped connection re-queues the unposted suffix intact. Uncovered because the real-wire lane cannot put the device offline and then make the server permanently reject a queued entry -- the constraint already recorded on errors.server-fault-is-not-offline, where no reachable failure can be manufactured without adding fault injection to the production app. Covering it needs a lane that can toggle connectivity and read the device queue. A dropped entry is also written to a bounded on-device quarantine (the most recent records only) and surfaced on the Habits screen as a count of the check-ins that could not be saved, dismissable by the user and wiped on logout, so the loss is no longer silent. The classification is pinned meanwhile by unit tests in src/features/Habits/services/__tests__/habitManager.test.ts and src/features/Habits/hooks/__tests__/useHabitActions.test.tsx, and the notice by src/features/Habits/components/__tests__/DroppedCheckInNotice.test.tsx.

In a build explicitly configured with EXPO_PUBLIC_HABIT_DEMO_MODE=true, with the habits fetch failing and no real cache, the app seeds ten demo placeholder tiles carrying fabricated ids 1-10, and those numbers are also the ids of whatever real rows the caller happens to own. A successful empty response never enters this mode. Every action on such a tile is local: revealing, reordering, renaming, changing the icon, resetting the start date, editing a goal or its shared units, logging a unit, opening stats, and -- the destructive one -- deleting. The tile changes or disappears in the store and nothing goes out, so a placeholder delete cannot become a DELETE against the user's own habit 3, and no "Couldn't sync" alert appears for something the user did only to themselves. A mixed store still performs each of those operations against the one genuinely server-backed row. Uncovered because the real-wire lane cannot produce the state -- it needs an explicitly demo-configured bundle and the habits fetch to throw while the cache is empty, while the lane's premise is a backend it can reach, the same constraint already recorded on habits.offline-check-in-replay-drains and errors.server-fault-is-not-offline. The same local-only rule covers every client-minted row, not just the demo family: onboarding scaffold rows and pre-sync added rows are marked hasClientMintedIds and may not put their provisional ids on the wire. A client-minted row is the user's real data, so it reaches the on-disk cache while a demo tile never does. Pinned meanwhile by unit tests in src/features/Habits/services/__tests__/serverIds.test.ts, src/features/Habits/services/__tests__/habitManager.test.ts, and src/features/Habits/hooks/__tests__/useHabitActions.test.tsx.

A habit added after onboarding takes the next rung on the program cadence rather than the day it was added, so the row sits where a reorder pass would put it and carries the date its stage badge has always implied. The second half is the one that moved other screens: a row stamped today could undercut a start date the user picked in the future, because when no anchor is stored -- after a logout wipes it, or for an account that onboarded before the anchor existed -- the universal anchor Map, Practice, Course and Journal all read is re-derived as the minimum over program rows, and a today-stamped add won that minimum. The covering Playwright spec pins the browser to UTC, signs up through the UI and seeds two program rows over POST /habits/ on the rungs of an anchor thirty days in the future, then reloads so the journal derives that anchor -- which the Map confirms before anything is added: stage 2 reads Unlocks in 51 days. It adds a habit through the Habits drawer's Add Habit sheet and reads two things that can fail. On the wire, the sheet's POST /habits/ carries the third rung (anchor + 42 days), not today, and GET /habits/ echoes that start_date on a program row. On screen, after a real log-out from Settings -- the spec checks the stored anchor is gone -- and a log-in through POST /auth/login, the anchor is re-derived from the rows, the added one among them, and the Map still reads Unlocks in 51 days; a today-stamped add would make it read 21. No habit tile renders a date, the reorder modal re-lays every program row on the cadence the moment it opens, and the web date picker in habit settings renders nothing, so none of those is the observation. Pinned in process as well by src/features/Habits/services/__tests__/habitManager.test.ts (the "addHabit lays a program row on the cadence" block, which covers the stored anchor, the absent-anchor fallback, the day-one case, the carryover partition, the reload that follows the add, and the saturation past ten stages that this deliberately shares with the reorder modal).

The date the user picks in Energy Scaffolding is the day their program begins, and it stays that day. They choose it in the reorder step, the scaffold rows POST with dates laid out from it, and the reload that follows re-derives the universal anchor that Map, Practice, Course and Journal all read for the current stage and week. A habit the user brought along from before the program carries the date they actually started it, which is usually earlier than the date they picked, and it must not become the program's beginning -- otherwise bringing one habit along on day one moves every other screen back to a day the program had not started. Uncovered because this lane runs on the node environment with node_modules untransformed and cannot mount a screen at all, the same constraint already recorded on welcome.first-run-walkthrough-to-journal: driving this journey means opening the scaffolding modal, operating its date picker, and adding a habit from the carryover lap, none of which a lane that cannot render can do. Pinned meanwhile by unit tests in src/features/Habits/services/__tests__/habitManager.test.ts (the "program anchor ignores carryover habits" block, which covers the live load, the offline cache, and the reload that follows onboardingSave) and by the picker's own label in src/features/Habits/components/__tests__/OnboardingModal.step4.test.tsx. Two anchors exist and this journey watches only the client's: the server stamps its own when the progress row is created, so a user who picks a future date has one of each and they disagree until they are reconciled.

A user opens Reorder Habits and performs a real browser pointer drag across the visible carryover/program boundary. Crossing that line changes the persisted is_carryover classification; after saving, the browser walks both pages and verifies that the remaining program habit keeps the ranked Beige stage color while the moved carryover tile and its progress use the unranked Candle & Ink accent. The component suite separately pins light/dark accents, achieved-state brightening, the -10 to -1, 1–10, and later-lap markers, plus program-date recalculation and carryover-date preservation.

A user first tries to save a page made only of whitespace, a zero-width mark, and a control character; the production client receives the stable journal_message_empty refusal and the live journal remains empty. They then write legitimate Unicode prose, find it in the list, and read the body back unchanged. The backend boundary suite separately sweeps spaces, tabs/newlines, controls, and zero-width-only bodies across create and edit, proving those refusals happen before a journal row, Creek write, corpus classification, pipeline run, or wallet event.

A writer saves a page, returns to the shelf, loses their connection, and opens that page anyway: the client short-circuits the GET, so the page shows its load-error banner and will not save (#2935). When the device comes back online, the real browser sees the load run again by itself, the banner clear, and the stored body appear; the writer then edits the page without reopening it, and the PATCH lands and is read back from the server. The seam suite JournalEntryScreenReconnectLoad.test.tsx pins what the browser cannot isolate: exactly one reload per offline-to-online edge and none while merely online, no duplicate or in-flight reload, a failed reload that retries only on the next edge, a fresh page that never loads, words typed while the entry was unloaded kept below the stored body and saved once, never auto-saved into a finished entry (the edit-confirm dialog says they are waiting and they save only after Edit), never saved under a looser stored tier than the one shown while typing (the entry is escalated first; page saves, the exit flush and Finish are held while it is in flight; if it fails the words stay off the page with a note and return only after a retry or the writer's own choice confirms a strict enough tier; a looser choice keeps them held), and no exit (Close, Back to reading, back gesture or hardware back) leaves held words behind without the writer's explicit choice in a Stay / Leave without them dialog, no stale pre-load debounce writing over the stored body, and no carry of those words into a different route entry. journalReconnectLoad.test.ts pins the reload gate and the carry rules term by term.

A writer sees that ordinary New entry still opens without a title, closes it, then takes the morning-pages invitation. The real browser lands on a fresh JournalEntry titled with that account/browser's local YYYY-MM-DD plus Daily Journal, and the writer can immediately replace the generated title. The shelf component test pins the exact prefillTitle navigation parameter, the tip test freezes a UTC instant across the prior-day America/Los_Angeles boundary, and the saved Journaling-practice quick-launch suite pins the same shared title contract.

A writer on a day with no review due sees the morning-pages tip with its Begin a page CTA, a quiet Don't show this again link beneath it, and an icon-only X in the card's top-right corner named Set the morning-pages tip aside (#2860). At 390x844 and 1280x720 the real browser measures the X flush with the band's top-right corner and inside it, at least 44px square, clear of the Begin a page button's box, of the never-again link's 44px-tall box and of every line of card text, and the card's label, title, body, CTA and link on one left edge, with no visible Not now. The X sets the tip aside for TODAY only, in the account's own time zone (#3005): pressing it by keyboard removes the card, lands focus on the Start a review early link rather than the page body, persists that day under the per-day set-aside key (never the retired permanent key), keeps the tip gone after a same-day reload, and brings it back after a reload with the browser clock on the next day in the account's zone. Component tests pin the close variant's accent-while-pressed tint, the begin area's corner reserve, the focus handoff's target, the Los Angeles 23:59/00:00 boundary under frozen clocks, the return on a later focus of a still-mounted shelf, and the legacy permanent flag's one-time migration.

A writer who wants no morning-pages invitation at all activates the tip's quiet Don't show this again link by keyboard, by its spoken name (Don't show this again: stop offering morning pages on the shelf), and the card goes, focus lands on Start a review early, and the device stores the permanent never-offer flag (#3005). The tip stays gone after a same-day reload and after a reload with the browser clock on the next day in the account's zone, where the X's set-aside would have lapsed. In Settings, the Journal group's Offer morning pages again row clears that flag and today's set-aside and says so in its description; back on the Journal shelf the tip is offered again. Component tests pin the link's action face at body weight in soft ink, its 44dp hit area and corner reserve, the save-then-focus order, the stale-read guard, and the Settings row's copy sweep.

A writer enters the journal's lightweight Markdown dialect, finishes the page, and sees asterisk-delimited bold text, underscore-delimited italics, <u>tag-delimited</u> underline (a retired ==equals== spelling stays literal prose), adjacent -/*/+ lines as one list block, and consecutive > lines as one quote block. The same rendering survives a cold reload while the exact source remains stored for editing and for code-point-based marginalia and promoted-quote anchors. The browser spec crosses the real editor, create/read routes, semantic web elements, and durable journal row; component coverage separately pins malformed text, literal HTML-looking prose, Unicode offsets, and anchors that cross hidden markers.

A writer sees the journal's Markdown rendered while they are still typing it -- a styled mirror over the real textarea draws bold, italics, <u>underline</u> and quote lines in place, block markers and delimiters dimmed rather than deleted and revealed around the caret -- and formats with Cmd/Ctrl+B/I/U or the toolbar. Browser undo and redo take a shortcut back, pasted Markdown is kept verbatim, and the stored body stays byte-identical to what was typed, so every marginalia / promoted-quote anchor still addresses the same code points. The spec types with the keyboard, checks the title is never intercepted, lets the page save, reloads into read mode, and separately probes that clicking a mirror glyph puts the textarea caret on that exact character at 390/768/1024/1440px in light and dark.

A writer nests a list from the keyboard: Tab indents the list item under the caret by the document's own unit, Shift+Tab outdents it, Return on an empty nested item steps out one level (and leaves the list at level 0), and Backspace at a nested item's content start steps out one level too. Tab on prose and Shift+Tab at level 0 are left to the browser, so focus always moves on. On a list line the toolbar offers Indent and Outdent. The stored body is exactly the indentation typed, and read mode draws the same nesting after a cold reload.

A writer types a fresh page and presses the always-available X before its debounced first save. The close waits for the create response before navigation lets the shelf refetch, the new page is visible immediately, and reopening it shows the exact body. A component regression test separately holds the create promise open to prove navigation ordering and verifies a rejected final write leaves the writer with the retry affordance.

A writer's page fails to save while the device is offline: an edited body and a stricter privacy tier both fail, the tier control reverts to what the server holds, and the footer says Couldn't save with a Retry. Coming back online re-sends both with no tap, the hint settles on Saved, and the server row and the reopened page carry the new body and tier. Online, a failed tier PATCH is recovered by pressing Retry. A tier looser than the one shown is never sent by a retry: it is dropped on reconnect and the page stays at its stricter tier until the writer chooses Public again. Jest seam suites (JournalEntryScreenSaveRetry, and the #2930 cases in JournalEntryScreenPrivacy, JournalEntryScreenChord and JournalEntryScreenFinish) pin the lanes the browser cannot isolate: Finish retried through the edit gate and never on reconnect, one lane's success never clearing another's failure, the single-flight create (#1144), and the retry's own single-flight.

A writer's first save of a new page, or their answer to the week's prompt, reaches the server but its answer is lost on the way back. The page cannot tell that from a save that never arrived, so it retries: first the transport (a keyed POST is retry-eligible), then the footer's Retry. Every attempt carries the one Idempotency-Key the page minted for that create, so the server answers each retry with the row it already stored rather than writing a second entry, and a lost prompt answer settles on Saved instead of being reported as the week already taken. Words typed after the lost create are PATCHed over the replayed row, so the one stored entry holds the newer text. The browser spec commits the first POST and drops its response, counting rows through the account's own API; Jest seam suites (the #2936 cases in JournalEntryScreenSaveRetry, saveFinishedEntry and JournalPhotographScreen) pin what the browser cannot isolate: a stricter tier re-asserted on the replayed row, a failed reconcile that leaves the page id-less, the photograph capture's own key, and a replayed answer holding older words staying honest as week-taken.

A writer opens a fresh Journal page whose title occupies one line before they type. A long title can still wrap visually, pasted line breaks collapse to spaces, and Return moves the caret into the body without becoming stored title data. Closing crosses the production client and create route, and the returned durable row carries the exact single-line title; schema tests separately pin the server-side defence for non-UI create and update callers.

A reader opens a finished entry, clicks through the one-time promote explainer a fresh account meets first (Choose the passage), sees the caret-hidden selection field light its accent focus rule on focus in place of the browser ring (#2952, WCAG 2.4.7), uses a real mouse selection to promote part of its text, sees the notice name where it went (Promoted — find it any time under Promoted quotes), sees the saved highlight after a cold reload, and removes it again. The journey crosses the rendered selection affordance, production promotions client, ownership-scoped routes, and durable quote row instead of proving the API in isolation.

The first time a reader taps Promote a quote, a note opens instead of the selection field: titled Promote a quote, it says a promoted passage waits among the sources of a review that covers the week it was written (what GET /reflections/sources does: a pending quote rides with its source entry, not with whichever review comes next) and can be seen any time under Promoted quotes in the Journal menu, with a real, unticked Don’t show this again checkbox and two arms whose rendered boxes are the same size on one row. Not now closes it with no selection field and nothing stored. Asked again, the reader ticks the box and chooses the passage; the selection field takes focus (the Promote button has unmounted with the read controls, so focus would otherwise fall to the page). The reader promotes a passage over the real route and the notice reads Promoted — find it any time under Promoted quotes in a polite live region. The dismissal is written to this account's scoped key (#u<id>), the Journal menu's Promoted quotes door lists the quote under Not yet in a review, and after a cold reload the next Promote a quote goes straight to a focused selection field. Not asserted in the browser, and pinned only by Jest: the press that lands before the stored flag has loaded waiting for it, a second account on the same device still seeing the note, and the iOS VoiceOver announcement. The in-sheet Promote a passage from this source opener in a review's sources panel is deliberately not gated by the note.

A reader on a phone opens an entry several screens long, taps Promote a quote, and selects a passage near its end. The mirrored field wears no browser focus ring and grows to its text instead of becoming an inner scroll pane, and the preview / Promote / Cancel footer stays pinned at the foot of the viewport (web position: sticky) while the body scrolls, so the confirm is in reach without scrolling past the whole entry. The browser spec seeds and finishes a 121-line entry over the API, opens it from the shelf at 390x844, clicks through the one-time promote explainer, and asserts the field has outline-style none, no inner scroll (scrollHeight <= clientHeight) and a height over three viewports; with the field's top at the top of the screen, the footer and Promote selection are in the viewport and pinned over the field. It then scrolls the closing line clear of the footer, drags a real mouse selection over it, and promotes it over POST /journal/{entry_id}/promote, whose stored anchor_text equals the preview. Native, where the footer stays in flow, is pinned by QuoteSelectionSurface.test.tsx and readingSurfaceStyles.test.ts.

On any day, not only inside a review composer, a writer opens the Journal drawer's 'Promoted quotes' door (a door with no count) and sees every quote they have promoted, grouped by status: 'Not yet in a review (n)' above 'Used in a review (m)', each header carrying the server's total for its own section. A quote seeded through the real promote route near the end of a long finished page is listed verbatim with its source title; tapping it opens that page in read mode scrolled to the passage, which is underlined and asserted in the viewport. Back on the screen, Remove asks first, the confirmed remove issues DELETE /promotions/{promotion_id}, and after a cold reload the screen shows the exact empty copy and GET /promotions returns nothing. Not asserted in the browser, and pinned only by Jest and pytest: the Write a review picker hand-off, per-section paging, the revert-in-place of a refused remove, the stale and deleted-review captions, refetch on refocus, and the cross-tenant and soft-delete exclusions of GET /promotions.

A due weekly review is opened from the Journal shelf, saved with its hierarchical identity (tag hierarchical_reflection, level week, scope key c1:w1), closed, and reopened as an ordinary saved entry. Its Sources affordance survives that reopen, and the panel names THAT review's own period -- read from the window the sources endpoint declares it filtered on -- so a reopen can never quietly present another review's material. Selecting a pending promoted quote folds it into the body, autosaves the reflection, and marks the quote included on the server. The spec drives the WEEK level only and asserts no title text. Review titles in the program's words are asserted elsewhere: the weekly titles under journal.review-from-the-shelf-cta, the section and course invitations and titles under journal.section-and-course-review-invitations; the stage invitation is pinned only by Jest. The sheet renders each source body through the journal Markdown model -- a '**Me:**' speaker prefix reads as bold 'Me:' and no raw marker ever appears in the collapsed excerpt or the expanded body -- and closes with an icon-only X whose accessible name is 'Done'. That the body grows to hold folded quotes at phone width, instead of painting them over the footer and rail, is asserted under journal.fold-selected-promoted-quotes (#3001).

A writer composing a due weekly review opens Sources, taps 'Select quotes', and the pending quotes become checkboxes whose state the browser reads from aria-checked. With nothing checked the fixed action reads disabled (aria-disabled). Two of three quotes promoted from one source are checked out of order; the action, which sits outside the scroll and stays in the viewport, reads exactly 'Fold 2 quotes into this review'. One press splices both as Markdown blockquotes attributed to the source title, in the order they sit in the source, one blank line apart, after the writer's own text; the review autosaves to 'Saved' and the server holds that exact body; exactly one PATCH /promotions/{promotion_id} per checked quote names the review's id, and the folded rows read as folded (aria-disabled). From the review's own Journal drawer the Promoted quotes screen then reads 'Not yet in a review (1)' and 'Used in a review (2)'; there 'Select quotes' turns the waiting quote into a checkbox, the fixed footer action reads 'Fold 1 quote into this review', and pressing it returns to the review, which folds that quote in once (each passage appears exactly once in the saved body) and marks it included on the review; the screen then reads 'Not yet in a review (0)' and 'Used in a review (3)'. At a 390x844 phone viewport, after a long typed opening and a two-quote fold with no keystroke after it, the body textarea reaches the last folded line the mirror draws, and the formatting toolbar, the save footer and the Finish rail start at or below the textarea's bottom -- a value written from the app re-measures the field just as typing does, so folded text never paints over them (#3001); Sources is an icon in the entry's exit row above the page, not on the rail (#3002). The toolbar trails that body taller than the phone: scrolled into view, it bolds a word the writer typed and selected at the end of the text. Pinned only by Jest, not asserted in the browser: one body change and one entry write per batch whatever its size; the partial-failure retry that re-marks only the refused quotes from the composer hint without splicing again; a failed mark's warning kept per quote, so another quote's overlapping successful fold never clears it and Try again re-marks only that quote; a quote removed meanwhile (its PATCH answers 404 promotion_not_found) retiring from the warning and the panel, and a retry marking before it splices so a removed quote's words are never put back (#2754); the duplicate-press and per-quote in-flight guards; identical blocks written once; Select all / Clear all, and on the screen Select all covering only the loaded rows with a visible note while older quotes remain; the selection surviving a resize across the side-pane breakpoint; the exact caret placements; the screen's 'Write a review with N quotes' arm (the review picker opens the chosen review, new or continued, which folds the selection in once after it hydrates); the hand-off token that only travels from a review being written; and a selection addressed to another page being left alone.

A writer composing a due weekly review opens Sources beside a week of long dailies and browses deep into the feed. The panel's heading -- the 'Sources' title, the period and the icon-only X named 'Done' -- stays fixed above a scroll that holds only the quotes and the feed, so at 390x844 and 1280x720 the X is still in the viewport and inside the panel after scrolling to the end, and it is at least 44x44. On a wide screen (1240 and up) the pane sits beside the writing sheet, never stacked full-width beneath it, and the entry body keeps a readable width and the sheet most of the height; narrower, a bounded sheet capped at the content width opens over the page. On the phone sheet the X, Escape and a tap on the backdrop each close only the panel, and after each focus returns to the Sources toggle; on the wide pane Escape does the same. Opened from the keyboard -- the toggle sits in the exit row above the editor (#3002) -- the pane and the sheet each put focus on their X, and Enter there closes the panel and hands focus back to the toggle. The route stays and the draft is untouched. Escape pressed while typing in the entry body belongs to the editor: the pane stays open and the writer keeps focus and keeps typing. The writer keeps typing, the page autosaves to 'Saved', and the server holds the continued text on the same entry id. At 390, 768, 1024 and 1440 nothing overflows horizontally, an expanded source stays readable, and closing gives the editor back its width. When a source enters quote selection, 'Promote selection' and 'Cancel' stay inside the panel at 390x844 and 1280x720. Not asserted in the browser, and pinned only by Jest: the Android hardware back button (the sheet's Modal request, the wide pane's BackHandler, which stands down while another screen covers the entry so back pops that screen), the expanded rows and in-progress selection surviving a resize across the side-pane breakpoint, and the native bound on the selection field.

A writer types formatted Unicode into the live editor -- a decomposed accent, a ZWJ emoji sequence the server strips, bold typed key by key, italics, underline, an escaped marker, a nested bullet, a leading newline and trailing spaces -- and finishes. Read mode promotes into the body the server STORED, not the typed one, and a selection's trailing space never reaches the stored span, so anchor_end - anchor_start equals the length of anchor_text. A resonance pass anchors a margin note. Two quotes folded into the due week review render as quote blocks in the live mirror at once, with exactly one blank line between them. The source is then edited before every anchor by typing formatting and by a list indent; on reopen the pending quote and the note each still address exactly their own text at the new code-point offset, and the folded quotes (whose offsets the server freezes) are listed apart rather than washed over other words. The review still renders both blocks after reopening.

On a wide read view (>= 600px) each margin note sits beside the passage it annotates rather than stacking from the top of the column: a long page given two resonance passes (the stub quotes the last sentence, so the second pass follows an appended sentence) opens with both notes far down, the first level with its highlight and each at the top computeMarginSlots gives its measured anchor, within a pixel. The two passages share a line, so the second note is pushed below the first by at least the margin gap, in document order. The margin column grows to hold the lowest note, which hangs past the end of the writing, and after scrolling journal-page-scroll to its end that note is wholly on screen -- the column stays inside the page's one shared scroll surface, never a scroller of its own. At 390px the margin stacks under the writing and keeps its document-order flow, no slot absolutely positioned. A refused check-off (the accept route answered 500) raises the margin's error banner above the notes, moving the stream without resizing it: the note is re-placed against its passage, and since the banner pushed the stream past that passage the note is held at the stream's top, clear of the banner. Pinned only by Jest: completion suggestions and undrawn (stale or overlap-skipped) notes trailing the anchored ones in creation order, a non-finite measurement trailing, the flow layout until every slot is measured, edit mode staying in flow, and a re-measure on the page's own layout. Not claimed: native alignment (native keeps the flow layout; onTextLayout measurement is a follow-up) and body-to-margin scroll sync or tap-to-scroll, which belong to #2893.

On a review day the Journal shelf's one call to write is the due review -- a button named by its visible words, 'Write your Weekly Review' -- and the daily-page tip steps aside; pressing it opens a fresh page titled in the program's own words ('Weekly Review -- Week 1'). On day 9, when nothing is due, the daily page holds that slot and the quiet 'Start a review early' link opens a picker of the scopes still in progress (GET /reflections/current); choosing the week opens 'Weekly Review -- Week 2', and the saved page carries scope c1:w2. Closing it and reopening the picker offers 'Continue -- Weekly Review -- Week 2', which reopens that same page (same body, still exactly one c1:w2 entry). Not asserted in the browser, and pinned only by Jest and pytest: the stage CTA (the section and course CTAs and titles are asserted under journal.section-and-course-review-invitations), dismissing a review, the no-card-while-loading rule, the picker re-reading on refocus, the 409 reroute to the live review, the stage-10 section omission, and the timezone-local day count. The review composer's sources feed is covered by journal.fold-promoted-quote-into-reopened-reflection, not here. The shelf band's eyebrow, its set-aside count and the 'Start a review early' link share one edge and one face (#2949); that alignment is pinned by Jest and its geometry is deferred to the #2948 text-order census.

A writer who finished the 36-week arc and began again reopens a review from their FIRST pass, at any level of the cadence -- a week, a stage, a section of three stages, or the whole course. The sources feed serves that cycle's own dailies, windowed against the anchor that cycle was lived under and clamped at the local midnight the loop happened, so the two laps abut rather than overlap and no entry from the new cycle appears under the old review's heading. A cycle whose anchor was destroyed by begin-again before this was fixed says its period cannot be reconstructed, rather than implying nothing was written then. The spec pins the browser to UTC, rewinds the anchor 230 days (20 days into stage 10) with tests.e2e.program_anchor, and lets a real GET /stages/program-calendar read record stage 10 in cycle 1; it then POSTs begin-again to the real route (the Map offers the button only at 100% stage-10 progress, which no lane writer produces) and asserts cycle 2 with cycle 1's anchor retained. With a finished first-pass daily (backdated 120 days), a DRAFT c1:course review and a finished cycle-2 daily that GET /reflections/sources for c2:w1 does serve, reopening the c1:course review from the shelf and opening Sources shows the first-pass daily and never the cycle-2 one; on the wire the window ends at the local midnight of the loop day, short of the course's natural 252 days, and the panel's period label names that declared window. With the anchor nulled by the out-of-band forget-past-anchor arrange (the state a pre-#2894 loop left), the feed is anchor_status unrecorded with no bounds and the panel shows the 'cannot be reconstructed' copy, with no period label and no empty-period copy. Sources is a writing-only door (#3002/#3004): it is opened on a draft review, and a FINISHED first-pass review opens to read with no Sources until Edit is pressed and confirmed. Pinned only by pytest and Jest: the week, stage and section levels, multi-loop index padding, and a review spanning weeks never lived (test_reflections_window.py, tests/domain/test_cycle_calendar.py, test_stages_api.py, ReflectionSourcesPanel.test.tsx).

On the last day of every third stage the Journal shelf offers a Section Review named after the Wavelength turn it closes (Red at stage 3, Green at 6, Ultraviolet at 9), and on the program's final day it offers the Course Review, whose sources decompose into the three sections plus the tenth stage that no section covers. Both moments became reachable only with issue #2866 -- before it, a third stage closed as a plain stage review and the final week closed as a "program" review. The spec pins the browser to UTC and rewinds the anchor in DAYS AGO, not 1-based program days: 62 days back is program day 63, the last of stage 3, where GET /reflections/due names section c1:x1, the shelf's one call to write is 'Write your Section Review' with 'Section Review -- Red' in its accessible name, the opened page is titled 'Section Review -- Red', and the saved page is exactly one c1:x1 entry tagged hierarchical_reflection at level section. 251 days back is program day 252, the final day, where c1:course is due: with finished c1:x1, c1:x2 and c1:x3 reviews, a finished daily backdated into week 1 and a finished daily written today (stage 10, week 36), GET /reflections/sources?level=course returns exactly the three section reflections then the stage-10 daily, in that server order, and never the week-1 daily that section 1 stands in for; the shelf offers 'Write your Course Review', the page is titled 'Course Review', and its Sources panel shows each section row under the 'Section reflection' eyebrow, the stage-10 daily, and no week-1 daily. The panel re-sorts the feed by time, so the decomposition order is asserted on the wire, not on screen. Pinned only by Jest and pytest: the Green and Ultraviolet sections and the stage CTA (JournalPrimaryInvitation.test.tsx), the whole-curriculum walk (tests/domain/test_reflection_hierarchy.py), the timezone-local day count and the period label (test_reflections_api.py, test_reflections_window.py).
A writer deletes one page from the shelf, the server stops serving it, and another account cannot delete it for them.

A writer whose Personal page and generated Voice Draft have reached their connected Creek vault deletes that page. The first content-free Voice Draft retraction fails at the real HTTP boundary, so Adepthood answers with its stable retryable withdrawal message and keeps the page visible instead of claiming success while derived plaintext remains. Repeating the same action after Creek recovers confirms both the AI-attributed draft and journal replica are absent before the local page disappears. The lane uses the production client and an out-of-process contract fake that records only opaque ids, tiers, actions, and digests; no journal or generated prose returns through its control surface.

Someone in the middle of a stage opens the Journal shelf and sees that stage's whole prompt set, each with the cadence the curriculum states for it, then taps one and writes against that prompt rather than against whichever question the week happened to draw. The seam is the ordinal: the page carries prompt_ordinal into the respond call, and the server decides whether that ordinal is one the stage actually carries. The second seam is the one-response-per-week rule: uq_promptresponse_user_week means a week holds a single response whichever prompt it answers, so the shelf stops offering a tap once this week's is written and the entry page says so if a save is refused anyway. Uncovered because no lane spec talks to the prompts routes yet, and a mocked client agrees with itself about the ordinal check, the stage's unlock gate, and the unique constraint -- the three things only the server can refuse.

A writer opens a page they finished days ago, asks for its resonance, and the reading lands in the margin against the words they actually wrote. The unhappy half is part of the journey rather than an edge case: a pass can legitimately keep nothing -- the model declines, or every quote it offers is a paraphrase that will not anchor -- and what the writer must never get is the outcome that was reported here, a button that visibly does nothing. So the journey ends either in a persisted note or in a sentence saying why there is none, with the charge reversed. Both endings are driven here against the configured default provider, which is the stub (BOTMASON_PROVIDER unset: no key, no network, no third party), so the route, the wallet, the anchoring and the rows are all real and only the model's sentences are canned; the stub declines exactly when the page gives it no sentence to copy, which is how the lane reaches the second ending. The spec also pins the privacy floor across the wire: an intimate page is answered before any provider is constructed, keeps no notes, and is not charged. What is NOT claimed is that any of it renders -- this lane runs on the node environment with node_modules untransformed and cannot mount JournalEntryScreen at all, the constraint recorded on welcome.first-run-walkthrough-to-journal. The margin's placement and its empty-state copy stay pinned by the Jest specs beside the screen; what crosses the seam here is that the note the margin will draw is one the server kept, anchored to characters the writer wrote. A pass also never runs over a copy whose latest write failed (#2980), nor while offline-typed words are held off the page (#2935): the screen's pass writer answers 'not saved' rather than the entry id, so nothing is generated or charged, the footer's Couldn't save / Retry keeps the save, the margin says the page has not saved (never 'write a little first'), and the next press after the save lands runs exactly one pass -- pinned client-side by frontend/src/features/Journal/__tests__/JournalEntryScreenResonanceDurable.test.tsx, since this lane cannot mount the screen.

A writer who has connected a vault -- ready, still provisioning, or with a stored host this server will not dial, or the deployment vault's bound owner -- asks for resonance. Their pass is answered by the vault or by nothing (#3061): a vault with nothing usable to say is a refunded zero-note pass with the server's own explanation; a vault that cannot answer (down, refusing, timing out, unreadable, no reflect capability, an unrecognized tier) is a refunded, retryable 503 reflection_source_unavailable whose margin copy says nothing was charged and the entry is saved; a locally distress-flagged entry gets the care surface alone; and completion detection, inside the pass and on the standalone route, answers checked: false. In none of those is the app's own model provider dialled, whatever BYOK key the request carries. Still uncovered as a journey: the wire lane's bound vault owner now crosses the real seam on the happy arm only -- journal-vault-withdrawal.e2e.test.ts asserts its margin note is the lane vault's own answer to POST /v1/reflections -- while none of the fail-closed arms above is driven over the wire yet; the out-of-process fake Creek vault (fakeCreekVault.mjs) is their future home. Pinned meanwhile at the route by backend/tests/security/test_vault_boundary_no_fallback.py, structurally by backend/tests/security/test_app_provider_construction_chokepoint.py, and client-side by useResonance.test.tsx and errorMessages.test.ts.

A writer's page screens as acute distress, and the resonance pass returns the care surface beside the reading (NORTH-STAR §10). The card opens on a short heading -- "You're not alone in this" -- with the four resources in server order, the 988 line first and Crisis Text Line second; the 988 row is asserted as a compact row that joins name and contact on one line and still says what the line is. An icon-only X in the card's corner removes the whole card: the journal page rises by at least the card's height less the one "Support options" line that stays in its place, and keyboard focus lands on that line instead of dropping to the page. That line restores all four resources in a single tap and puts focus back inside the card. Dismissing again and running a second distress-flagged pass re-shows the full card, because the dismissal is held in memory against that one care payload. Settings -> Support & care still lists all four resources afterwards. The care copy is the server's own reviewed payload crossing the real route on the lane's stub provider -- nothing about it is mocked -- and the page's rise and the focus handoff are measured in the browser because Jest has no layout or DOM focus.

A writer opens a finished page and presses Get Resonance for the first time. The press opens a disclosure before any request leaves the browser: what a pass does, that the entry's text, up to three other pieces of the writer's own writing, short excerpts of earlier letters, and the names and units of their habits and practices are sent to an AI model, and who pays. With no key, the rendered copy uses the deployment-served monthly cap and never promises that the allowance is free. The writer backs out, saves their own key through Settings, reopens the same page, and now sees that the key pays and neither BotMason bucket will move. Continue sends exactly one real request through the screen and production API to the lane's provider; its deterministic credit refusal proves the BYOK header arrived, while GET /user/usage proves both BotMason buckets stayed unchanged. The dismissal is then taken and the next press goes straight through without silently switching payer. Counted requests and server state keep the journey non-vacuous: a dialog-only assertion could pass while charging too early or charging both payers. This has to be the browser lane because the claim spans rendered presses and device key storage. Per-account namespacing of the dismissal flag remains pinned in the Jest specs beside the screen.

A writer can open API-key settings from the journal entry's exit row and return to the exact editor with its title and body intact. When the account has neither a monthly message nor an offering and no device key, Get Resonance opens a refill invitation naming the reset date instead of a disabled spend disclosure; its Add your API key arm reaches the same settings screen and returns without losing the draft. A second browser account makes the usage read stale, takes and dismisses the ordinary spend disclosure, and receives a real-shaped 402 from the pass: the refill invitation still replaces the old dialog, proving the dismissal flag cannot suppress the recovery path. A third holds the initial wallet response while the writer uses the live Settings form to save a lane key, then proves the mounted entry publishes only the new BYOK payer when that obsolete zero-wallet response arrives. A fourth holds an accepted resonance POST, opens and saves API-key settings, then releases a key-required 402 and proves the obsolete request cannot portal a funding invitation over Settings or the preserved entry. The browser intercepts only the deterministic wallet arrangements and funding failures; navigation, editor state, key storage/context, modal decisions, API client parsing, and request count all run through production code.

A note's first letter is a charged depth under the owner-ratified launch economy (#623): one wallet unit to write it, nothing to reopen it. Opening a note with no letter shows an offer, not a request: what a letter is, that the entry goes to an AI model, the price for the payer in force (the writer's own key, the monthly allowance by its served cap, or an offering), and equal-weight Ask for the letter / Not now arms. Only Ask sends POST /journal/marginalia/{marginalia_id}/essay, with price_acknowledged: true. Across the real wire, a server-paid ask without the acknowledgement is refused 409 essay_price_unacknowledged and moves neither the wallet nor its audit trail; the acknowledged ask spends exactly one monthly unit (one spend_monthly row, no refund) and its answer carries the same remaining_messages, remaining_balance and monthly_reset_date that GET /user/usage then reports; reopening the cached letter, acknowledged or not, is free. Pinned by Jest rather than this lane: the offer's copy and a11y, no ask on open, a cached letter opening straight to the letter, and an essay 402 routing to the pass's refill dialog. Pinned by the backend suite rather than this lane: the exhausted-wallet 402 before any provider call, and refunds for failed and empty letters.

Resonance or essay refused by a generation guardrail shows honest copy and costs nothing (#623). Under the owner-ratified limits (decision record §1: maximum 5 LLM generations/minute/user, maximum 2 concurrent generations/user, a configurable launch ceiling of 100 charged generations/day/user), a pass or a first letter asked for while two of the writer's generations are in flight is refused 429 generation_in_progress, and one past today's ceiling 429 daily_generation_limit_reached with Retry-After to the next UTC midnight; neither charges the wallet, writes an audit row or dials a provider. The margin line and the essay modal announce the refusal's own copy (wait for the one in flight; resets at midnight UTC), never the 402 refill invitation, and the essay modal offers no retry for the daily one. Uncovered because no e2e seam can put the account into either state: the daily ceiling counts walletaudit rows and the e2e lane has no database-seeding seam (the frontend has no pg client), lowering BOTMASON_DAILY_GENERATION_CEILING on the shared e2e server would refuse every other resonance spec, and holding two generations open needs a provider double the server lane does not expose. Pinned meanwhile by backend tests/routers/test_generation_guardrails_api.py (every refusal's 429, no charge, no dial, slot release on every exit) and by Jest: ResonanceEssayModal.test.tsx, JournalEntryScreenResonanceExplainer.test.tsx, generationRefusal.test.ts and errorMessages.test.ts.

A writer asks for resonance on a short saved entry that explicitly says they completed a tracked habit. The literary pass is refused at the browser boundary, but the production client still runs its independent completion check against the live server, renders both an honest reflection error and the habit offer, and accepting the offer persists the check-in. Detection also records the amount and the user-local day when the entry states them, so the accept logs that amount on that day rather than the goal's target on today; an entry stating neither behaves exactly as before. The literary refusal is deterministic route interception; detection, suggestion persistence, acceptance, and completion are real-wire behavior. The card states those facts before the writer consents rather than only after: the spec asserts the pending offer reads the amount and the day it will log, that the accept button a screen reader announces names them too, and that the persisted goalcompletion row carries that amount on that day rather than the goal's target on today. Once settled, the card names the day the server recorded the accept as logging (the suggestion's persisted logged_on, equal to goalcompletion.local_day), never a day re-derived from the detected day and the live clock: the spec asserts the settled text names that day straight after OK, and again after the entry is reopened the next day and hydrated from the suggestion list alone. The arm where the detected day differs from the logged day (a future or out-of-window detection that fell back to today) is not producible over the real wire, so it is pinned by JournalEntryScreenSuggestions and suggestionFacts instead.

A writer asks for resonance and, when their connected Creek vault recognises a compiled praxis or a recurring eddy in the entry, finds those related pages offered in a collapsed, display-only band beside the journal page. Expanding it shows the page titles, quiet lifecycle or fragment context, and excerpts without turning a pattern into a task. Empty and pre-vault responses leave no band behind. The reflection provider is no longer what blocks this: the lane's default provider now answers a resonance ask with an anchored reading, which is what journal.ask-for-resonance drives. What is still missing is the other half of the response -- a Creek vault fake, connected to the account and seeded with compiled praxis and eddy pages, that answers the reflection with related collections. The activation journey's fake Creek control plane allocates a vault; it does not serve a corpus. The component, hook, and rendered-screen contracts are pinned by the Jest specs beside JournalEntryScreen, and #2408 stays open for this seeded-vault seam.

A writer who has never decided about their corpus asks for resonance on a finished page and, once the reflection has actually landed in the margin, finds beside the page -- never in it -- a quiet note saying reflections can draw on their own earlier writing, what agreeing sends where and how often, and that a yes also sorts what is already written. They can look at the decision, set it aside with Not now, or say Do not ask again; every one of those is one tap, none of them touches the pass, and the answer is kept on the server so it holds across devices and does not return on the next press. On a plain Not now the note returns only after both seven days and three further completed passes; on Do not ask again, or once consent is decided either way, never. The pass count the cooldown runs on never reaches the client. Uncovered as a rendered moment: this journey is about the note appearing beside the page after the pass, and the real-wire lane drives the production client, not the screen. The wire half -- a completed pass opening the offer, and the decline being the server's to remember -- is covered by corpus.decline-the-offer-and-be-left-alone; the rendered half is pinned by the Jest specs beside JournalEntryScreen (placement, one-tap decline, the pass never gated) and by backend/tests/test_resonance_endpoints.py::TestACompletedPassIsCounted for which passes count. The provider seam is no longer what blocks it -- journal.ask-for-resonance now drives a pass that keeps real notes against the default stub provider, and this journey's remaining gap is only the rendered moment, which needs a lane that can mount the screen. #2408 stays open for it rather than being closed by the spec that covered the pass.

A writer who has never decided about their corpus completes a first resonance pass and is offered the decision; they set it aside with Not now and are not asked again on the very next pass; later they say Do not ask again, and a softer Not now afterwards does not undo it. A cold login on a fresh session reads the same standing, because the decision is the server's to remember rather than the device's; a request with no session is refused; and a neighbour's account is still un-asked until its own first pass opens its own offer. The pass that opens the offer is real -- the lane's provider is the stub, so it resolves as a refunded no-notes 200, which is still a completed pass by design -- so the seam this spec pins is the whole of it: the settlement counting the pass, the read the note makes, the verb and shape of both declines, and that the count itself never crosses the wire. Both halves are green on their own -- the note's tests mock the client, the router's tests never see it -- and this is the one place they agree.
A practitioner logs a practice session and finds it in the week's record.
A practitioner who sat without the app logs that sitting afterwards, choosing when it ended and how long it ran, and finds it counted in the week it happened.

A practitioner runs the stage-1 grounding ritual to its end, saves it with a one-line insight, and watches the weekly bar move from 0 of 4 to 1 of 4 in the page they are already looking at. The bar was wired correctly on both sides and still showed the pre-save number: the client incremented optimistically and then refetched, the server counted the new row, and in between GET /practice-sessions/insights advertised max-age=60, so the browser answered the post-save refetch out of its own HTTP cache and put the bar back to zero. No node-lane spec can see that -- node's fetch keeps no HTTP cache, so the request the browser answers for itself is the one the node lane always puts on the wire. This journey runs in the Playwright lane against a real server for exactly that reason, and asserts the server's own week-count alongside the rendered number so a failure separates a lost save from a display that lies about one.

A practitioner who has sat one practice several times walks from the player to that practice's own detail screen -- Practice, its drawer, "Practice details" -- and reads how much they have put into it: total sittings and total time, rendered as hours plus the minutes past 60. The totals are a backend aggregate keyed on an adoption the caller owns, never a client-side sum over a paged session list, and the aggregate widens server-side to every adoption of the same catalog practice that caller owns, so a practice carried from one stage into the next reports one lifetime figure rather than a per-stage slice. The spec logs a zero-length abort alongside two real sittings and asserts it moves neither number, which is the counting rule this endpoint had to settle: the insights rollup skips zero-duration rows, the legacy week-count route does not, and a total cannot honour both. It runs in the Playwright lane because the node lane cannot mount a screen at all (#2324), and because the rollup is read one tap from the player that writes the rows it counts -- the #2654 hazard, which only a browser holding an HTTP cache can see, so the last leg leaves the screen and comes back to force a real re-read.

A practitioner browsing the Practice tab's embedded catalog taps a practice and reads its details in an overlay on that tab rather than on a pushed screen, so the catalog they had narrowed (stage, mode, search, scroll) is still there when they decline: Escape on the web, the Android back button, the corner X or the scrim all close only the overlay, and focus returns to the row that opened it. Choosing the practice from the overlay writes a real adoption and flips straight to the player with it live, never popping a stack that was never pushed. The in-place Practice | Catalog flip the walk crosses in both directions cross-fades (#1952): the surface being left stays mounted, out of reach of touch and assistive tech, for one motion.threshold and then unmounts, which the spec checks under the browser's own animation driver; the fade's timing, reduced-motion swap and fail-open floor are pinned in Jest. The details come from the real GET /practices/{practice_id} and the choice from the real POST /user-practices/, which the Jest suite mocks and the node lane cannot mount a screen to reach. The overlay is not a route, so the browser's back button leaves the tab rather than closing it -- an accepted limitation the spec deliberately does not assert on.

A practitioner starts a meditation timer from the Practice screen and hears the session open, pass its halfway mark, and close, then logs the sitting. Uncovered, for two reasons rather than the usual one. The first is the familiar one: this lane runs on the node environment with node_modules untransformed and cannot mount a screen at all (#2324). The second is specific and is the reason this entry exists at all -- audibility is not assertable anywhere in this repository. There is no frontend/ios and no frontend/android, so nothing here runs on a device, and the two surviving acceptance criteria of #1419 ("a session audibly strikes start/half/end on device" and "bowl/chime/gong are three distinguishable sounds") are owner sign-off items. What ships in their place are substitutes, and they are named as substitutes: a peak-amplitude assertion on the rendered PCM, and a Goertzel dominant-frequency separation between all six timbres, in bellSynth.test.ts. Those prove the bytes are not silence and not the same bell twice; they do not prove a human in a room hears a bell. The bug this journey was written against is exactly the gap between those two claims -- six 0-byte mp3s resolved to valid modules, constructed players without throwing, and played nothing, so the failure was invisible to the user and to the logs alike, and the component test that was meant to guard it asserted only that a player had been constructed.
A practitioner submits a custom practice and adopts it as one they can actually do.

A reader opens a stage's content, reads a piece, and marks it read so progress moves. Which stage it opens on is the server's answer, not a count of completed stages the client makes for itself. The cold start's bounded wait is a state of this journey, not a journey of its own: it crosses no screen, client wrapper, route or table this entry does not already name -- it is a client-side timer over the same GET /stages read, and it is reached precisely when that read never answers, which no lane against a live server can arrange. Pinned in-process by src/features/Course/__tests__/CourseScreenColdStart.test.tsx, the way the Map's identical bounded wait is pinned by MapScreenColdStart.test.tsx and declared nowhere in this ledger.

A reader in a desktop browser opens a chapter, chooses Write a note on a passage, selects a passage by keyboard, double-click, and pointer drag, confirms Write a note, lands in JournalEntry with the passage prefilled as a blockquote, and waits for the entry to save. The covering Playwright spec boots the real Expo web app and FastAPI app over loopback against an alembic-built throwaway Postgres database; it exists because the Node API lane cannot exercise native textarea selection or browser accessibility semantics.

A reader finishes a chapter, marks it read, and taps Reflect in Journal. The writing surface opens already titled for the stage and the chapter, the reflection saves, and the way out is the way in: Back to reading returns them to that same chapter instead of leaving them on the Journal shelf to find the Course tab by hand. Sibling to course.write-note-on-passage, which drives the reader's other hand-off; this one is the reflection, which closes the reader behind it and so returns to the chapter rather than to a scroll position. It runs in the browser lane because the whole journey is screen-to-screen navigation -- the returnTo that makes the exit exist never crosses the wire, so no amount of API driving could see whether it is there. Verified to be a live gate rather than a passing formality: with the returnTo removed from handleReflect the spec fails on the absent Back to reading control.

A user whose first page of habits is full opens Habits in a desktop browser and, after a viewport flip to a phone profile, in one column. The covering Playwright spec signs up through the UI, seeds ten habits over POST /habits/ with a token from POST /auth/login, and then measures laid-out DOM: the grid's box ends at or above the top of both the pagination bar and the Energy Scaffolding CTA, and every tile lies inside the grid's box -- the first before any scrolling, the last after scrolling the grid to its end. It exists because the Jest lanes cannot answer a layout question at all: this project runs the node environment under the React Native preset, so onLayout never fires and every box is zero, which is why issue #2658's report of a grid "clipped beneath fixed controls" survived a green suite. Nothing here asserts that a full page fits without scrolling; the same spec measured 147px of overflow at 1280x720 and 129px at 390x844, and records those numbers on every run instead of claiming a fit the app does not hold.

A traveller opens the Map after the calendar has moved them into a new stage, and the server agrees they moved. Advance is not an action a person takes: the calendar over the ratified 21x8+42x2 schedule decides what is offered, and reading the Map records that the person entered it. There is deliberately no tap affordance -- a manual advance contradicts the earned, server-derived progression model -- so the covering spec moves the program anchor in the lane's own database and then reads, never posts. The three reads below are the whole of what the Map asks for: GET /stages/{stage_number}/progress is served but unreachable, and naming it here described a seam the app has no half of. Unlocking alone would prove nothing, because access is the union of the calendar and the record; so the spec asserts the record itself -- current_stage, completed_stages, stage_started_at -- moved when the Map was read, stayed put when the anchor moved without a read, and re-recorded nothing on a second read inside the same window.

A traveller opens the current stage on the Map and takes its strongest action, Continue, directly into that stage's Course chapter. The stage modal offers Course exactly once through that primary action; Practice and Journal occupy the two secondary slots, so no destination is duplicated. The component journey separately pins the stage-number route parameter and the close-before-navigation/double-tap guard, while this real-browser journey proves the rendered accessibility name, action hierarchy, modal dismissal, tab hand-off, and selected Course cover together.

Someone reads the Map at any viewport and every stage annotation stays legible: the Aspect word, a locked stage's padlock and "Unlocks ..." estimate, and a finished stage's check badge each stay off the wave's painted stroke, off each other and on screen, inside their own stage's cell and band, and a window too short for the table scrolls it rather than painting one stage onto the next (#2657); the lens's own caption -- the YOU ARE HERE chip, the stage title and subtitle -- stays on the glass, inside the rim and clear of the pill's rounded ends, so a caption set larger must grow the pill (#2960). Every grid size is a ramp step (#2960): stage copy that fits no step wraps at the 13px caption floor instead of shrinking, and each stage's left and center cells share one row that never shrinks below the taller cell's content, so a wrapped line or a long unlock estimate grows its own stage rather than spilling into the stage stacked with it; the right label is inset inside its cell, which is left unpadded so the columns keep the 2/2/1 flex split the wave is drawn to. Every line of every right-column aspect label reads whole -- never cut to an ellipsis -- and inside its own band: a label too wide for its cell by the glyph estimate falls back to its hyphenated lines (Aware- / ness on every standard phone from 320 to 414 wide, Under- / standing, Yes-And- / Ness), and no label line is capped with numberOfLines, so a line that runs wider than the estimate on any serif face wraps rather than truncating; a fifth test sweeps this rule across every phone width from 320 to 390 in 5px steps. At a desktop window the completed Map scrolls by no more than Begin again's button, so the whole table and Begin again's words read without scrolling; the top stage's cell takes no extra height for the lens when it is current, since the lens then overhangs only stage 9's UNITY watermark. The covering spec measures three states -- fresh (stage 1, stages 2-10 locked), partial (stage 5, stages 1-4 finished, second cycle so the cycle caption shows) and completed (stage 10 finished, Begin again showing) -- at 1280x720 and 390x844, plus a 1280x560 window for fresh and completed, each in one settled frame: two animation frames, then the text census and a sample of every wave path every 2px of arc (getPointAtLength through getScreenCTM) in the same evaluate. The current stage moves the only way it can, through tests.e2e.program_anchor (90 and 240 days back); per-stage completion has no writer at all, so the spec lets GET /stages and GET /stages/program-calendar reach the lane's server and rewrites only progress and cycle_number on the response -- nothing on the Map is stubbed. Before any rule runs it proves it measured something: a wave with length, and exactly as many unlock lines, padlocks in each column and badges as the state has locked and finished stages. The rules are pure functions in frontend/e2e/mapGeometry.ts pinned by src/design/__tests__/mapGeometry.test.ts. Each measure waits for its state to be established -- the calendar's stage in the journey read and under the lens's YOU ARE HERE chip, the cycle caption, Begin again -- and asserts those markers in the measured frame. A fourth test drags the lens with real touches (Input.dispatchTouchEvent in a touch context at 390x664, where the fresh Map scrolls): the lens moves and the Map's scroller stays put, while the same gesture on the table's text does scroll it. The magnifier pill and the EMPTINESS / UNITY watermark the converging wave rises through by design are the only intended covers. Screenshots and the measured frame land in e2e/artifacts/map-legibility/ for review; there is no pixel baseline.

Someone turns a depth ring on or off and the app they come back to is the one they chose: Habits, Practice and Course each add or remove their primary destination; Sangha adds or removes the Digital Sangha door in Settings (SanghaSection.tsx), and its switch is offered only in a build with EXPO_PUBLIC_SANGHA_INVITE_URL configured, because a switch with nothing to close would be a false choice. The live-wire spec proves enable_sangha round-trips independently; the in-process pairing of each switch with its destination is pinned by src/features/Settings/__tests__/depthSwitchesHaveEffect.test.tsx.

A person who HAS connected a vault chooses a document from their device and seeds it there -- since #3017 the picker is offered only to an account the server does not say has nothing attached, so an account with no vault is shown where its corpus lives first (corpus.bring-in-your-writing-needs-a-vault-first); the import forwards to the vault rather than persisting locally, so authentication is the only table it crosses. One route serves every account -- POST /corpus/import decides per account -- and this entry is the vault half of that decision; the no-vault half, answered vault_required with nothing stored (#3016), is corpus.import-without-a-vault. The lane now has a vault to reach: a loopback process answering Creek's published GET /v1/capabilities and POST /v1/uploads, reached through adepthood's own production CREEK_VAULT_URL and bound to one pre-provisioned account by CREEK_VAULT_OWNER_USER_ID. That binding is what closed the last blocker -- the variable is read from the server's environment and so names an id fixed before any account exists, which globalSetup settles by signing that account up as the lane's first request and refusing the whole run if the id it gets back is not the one already named. The deployment-wide value is also the only one that may name loopback: a user-supplied vault URL is refused unless it names a globally routable destination, which is why the connect-your-own path cannot serve this. The spec proves the seam end to end -- accepted with a ref, a re-send reported as one fragment edited in place rather than a second, and an Intimate document withheld before the vault is contacted at all, asserted against the vault's own record of what arrived.

Someone the server finds no vault for brings in a document they wrote elsewhere. A corpus lives in a vault (owner ruling on #3015), so since #3016 the answer is vault_required and nothing else happens: the document is not read, consent is not consulted, no provider is called and nothing is stored -- destination corpus, stored false, fragment_id null, vault fields null. The spec proves the document was never looked at by sending each thing the retired local import used to answer differently -- a .md with no consent, a .pdf, the same .md after turning the switch for documents on, an Intimate document, and a neighbour who agreed to nothing -- and getting the same answer every time.
