It still crosses PUT /corpus/consent/{source} on purpose: flipping the switch is how it proves the switch now lets nothing in.

Someone brings in a batch and leaves the screen before it has all gone over. The screen asks first rather than silently discarding the run, and confirming genuinely stops it: the document already in flight finishes wherever it lands, and everything still queued is never sent. The point of the journey is the seam, not the prompt -- what has to be proved is that the account's vault afterwards holds exactly the documents that had settled on screen (an account with no vault keeps nothing at all since #3016, each item settling as vault_required, so only a vault account has anything to read back), because the defect this closes was a run that kept uploading in the background while the person saw an empty screen. Covered at the hook and screen level by Jest (useSeedRun, useSeedLeaveGuard, SeedCorpusScreen), which can only assert that the client stopped calling the route; uncovered here because no spec yet reads the corpus back to confirm the server agrees.

A corpus lives in a vault (owner ruling on #3015), and since #3016 the server keeps nothing a vault-less account sends, so 'Bring in your writing' waits for a place to keep what comes in (#3017). In Settings the Your corpus group now leads with Where your corpus lives; for an account GET /vault/connection says has nothing attached, the seed row keeps its name and icon but says where that place is set up, and opens Where your corpus lives rather than the picker. Unknown -- a read still out, a read that failed, or a provider-managed vault answered with no address -- is never read as none and keeps the picker, with the server's vault_required as the backstop. The spec drives this unstubbed on a fresh lane account, which has no vault of its own and is not the deployment binding's owner. The Journal band (CTA 'Give your corpus a place to live'), the Journal drawer's Your corpus door and the seeding screen's own invitation take the same rule and are pinned in their component suites (VoiceReadinessBand, JournalEntryScreenDrawer, JournalShelfScreenDrawer, SeedCorpusScreen). Known gap: the deployment binding's single owner has no connection row and so is shown the same invitation although their imports land.

Someone takes a copy of everything they have written: they open Export my data, the app downloads the JSON archive and the Markdown journal, saves both to the device and offers them to the share sheet. The archive carries their own entries as prose, never another account's, and never the ciphertext the column holds. Beta feedback reports (the feedbackreport table) travel in the same archive under feedback_reports; that half is proven at the seam by feedback.admin-triage-inbox.

Someone saves their own OpenAI or Anthropic key on the device, then uses a model-powered feature. The production app sends the key over HTTPS to Adepthood in the X-LLM-API-Key header, and Adepthood forwards it over HTTPS to the selected provider for that request without persisting, logging, or returning it. Both Settings surfaces disclose those two service boundaries before the key is used. The copy and wire contract are pinned together by src/features/Settings/__tests__/byokDisclosure.test.ts and the rendered-screen specs beside it. The real-wire lane cannot cover the whole journey because it neither mounts SecureStore-backed Settings screens nor sends a live credential to an external model provider; doing so would turn a test fixture into a production secret and a billable third-party call.

Someone who saved their own model key on this device removes it from Settings. The press opens a rendered confirmation (not Alert.alert, which react-native-web ships as an empty method and which left the key irremovable on web, #2928); Cancel keeps the key and Remove clears it, and it is still gone after a reload. Removal itself is device-local and calls no route, so the journey proves what removal is for, on both ways the client picks a key, reached from the entry's own API-key shortcut in the same browser session. The resonance pass passes its disclosed payer explicitly: after removal it is disclosed as the shared allowance, leaves without the X-LLM-API-Key header, and raises monthly_messages_used by one, which catches a build that hid the card while the key stayed in context. The margin-note essay passes no key and so reads the session getter ApiKeyContext registers: opened after removal and before any reload, it too leaves without the header, which catches a build whose in-memory getter kept returning the removed key (the explicit-key pass cannot, since it never consults the getter). Controls made while the key is stored carry the header -- the pass itself, and the completion check the refused pass runs through the getter -- so the header's later absence is observed rather than assumed. The controls are answered in the browser and never reach a server, and the spec asserts the lane fake provider's shared attempt counters are unchanged at its end, because later specs require them to start at zero.

Someone opens the corpus-consent screen, finds every kind of material off and un-asked, turns their journal on, and later turns it back off -- which deletes the copies it collected and leaves a dated refusal on the record rather than an open question. Turning it on now reaches backwards as well: the entries already in their journal are sorted on the same terms as a new one, bounded so the request they are waiting on stays finite. The spec covers the switch and the deletion; what it cannot yet observe is the reach, because the lane has no classification provider, so a backfilled entry settles as unclassified and writes no fragment for a spec to see. A provider that refuses to bill now ends that reach rather than consuming the queue, and never costs the person the permission they just gave -- the switch still answers granted and the entries it did not get to keep their place. The backend pins it at backend/tests/test_corpus_consent_api.py.

Someone ends their account from inside the app: they read what goes and what stays, retype their own address to confirm, and the server erases them and hands back a receipt. The receipt's vault half is account-scoped rather than deployment-scoped. This lane does have a deployment-wide vault for seed.upload-document, but globalSetup binds that single corpus to one pre-provisioned owner; the later account created by this journey has no per-user connection and must therefore receive `configured: false` with no-vault guidance, never a claim on the other person's vault. Backend API regressions separately pin manual owner, per-user connection, unconfigured, and provisioned teardown receipts. Erasure takes the account's beta feedback reports (feedbackreport) with it; that half is proven at the seam by feedback.admin-triage-inbox, where the operator can no longer open or list them.

A feature screen throws while a journal entry is on screen; the boundary shows the recovery card, "Try again" remounts the subtree, and the crash report that leaves the device carries none of what was written. Still uncovered because the e2e lane cannot mount a screen at all: it runs on the node environment with node_modules untransformed, so importing the boundary dies on @react-navigation/native's ESM and react-native's Flow syntax, and the lane's own guard pins the moduleNameMapper to the @/ alias so the React Native preset cannot be added to a spec. Observing the outgoing crash envelope is banned in this lane by the same guard. Covering it needs a second, rendering lane, not another spec here.

The server hits an unhandled exception while the journal shelf is loading; the app says something went wrong on our end and offers the server's request id as a reference, instead of telling the user to check their wifi. Each side is pinned separately: backend/tests/middleware/test_unhandled_exception_cors.py drives the real app and asserts the 500 leaves it carrying Access-Control-Allow-Origin, and src/api/__tests__/serverErrorIsNotOffline.test.ts asserts the client keeps the sanitised envelope's code and request id while a failure that produced no response at all reads as the server being unreachable. That last arm changed with #2661: a request a browser blocks on CORS and a request that reaches nothing are the same bare TypeError to JavaScript -- measured in Chromium, identical message, properties, and resource-timing entry -- so the copy no longer diagnoses the device, and the "you appear to be offline" claim is raised only behind the client's own connectivity signal. Both arms are pinned in src/api/__tests__/corsRejectionIsNotOffline.test.ts. Uncovered here because the real-wire lane has no way to make the live server 500 — every reachable failure is a deliberate 4xx or 503, and adding a fault-injection route to the production app to manufacture one would be worse than the gap.

A device that already holds one account's session is signed into by a second account without an explicit logout -- through the password-reset flow, or any path that reaches the login screen with a live cache on disk. The incoming user must see none of the previous user's habits, none of their check-in queue replayed under the new token, and none of their BYOK key on the resonance header. Uncovered because the leak is a row on the device rather than a row on the server: this lane drives HTTP against a live backend from Node, with no app process and therefore no AsyncStorage or SecureStore to seed, dirty, or read back, so a spec written against the wire could only assert that the backend scopes reads to its caller -- which it already did throughout, and which was never the failing half. Held meanwhile by src/context/__tests__/AccountSwitchWipe.integration.test.tsx, which drives the real AuthProvider and the real habitStorage against the in-memory AsyncStorage mock, plus the per-account namespacing tests in src/storage/__tests__/. The cold start behind that door is held by src/context/__tests__/ResumedSessionScope.integration.test.tsx, which pins the namespace a resumed session reads to the subject of the token it resumed rather than to a separately persisted stamp the two non-atomic sign-in writes can leave disagreeing. What that meanwhile-guard holds now includes the device-cached timezone: the switch drops the outgoing account's zone, and drops it before the incoming account's is written to the same unscoped device key, so a failed write cannot leave the previous account's calendar driving the next one's day boundary.

A writer asks for resonance while the balance behind the key that pays for it is spent. What they got was "the AI provider is having trouble connecting, give it a moment and tap retry" -- a transient story for a permanent, billing-level refusal, so the retry button they were pointed at could never work and the real cause reached nobody. The journey now ends in copy that names the condition and the one action that clears it, split by whose key it was, with no retry affordance and the charge reversed; on the server's own key an operator gets the WARNING that is their first signal it happened at all. The browser spec presses "Get Resonance" against the real server for both halves -- the caller's own key (402) and, through the token-gated provider probe, the server's own key (503) -- and neither half raises the typed error: the lane points the production SDK clients at a loopback fake through their own OPENAI_BASE_URL / ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, so openai.RateLimitError and anthropic.BadRequestError are built by the SDKs out of the providers' real refusal bodies, which is the classification the bug turned on. The same spec drives the counterweight -- a genuine rate limit, same provider and same 429 with a different code, which keeps its transient copy and its retry -- proves an intimate page still reaches no provider with one armed, and reads walletaudit out of band to show the pass was charged and put back rather than never charged. Each side is still pinned separately: backend/tests/services/test_botmason_credit_exhausted.py drives both SDKs through a mock transport so each builds its own typed error from the provider's real body, backend/tests/test_resonance_endpoints.py asserts the 402/503 split and the operator record, and src/api/__tests__/errorMessages.test.ts asserts neither code inherits the transient copy.

Someone who made their own practice tag renames it, and later deletes it, from the recipe editor's tag library. The library could list and create and stopped there, so both routes were served, typed, and unreachable from any screen. The journey is the seam: that a rename reaches the row the client named and survives the next list rather than living in local state, that the slug a recipe step copied by value is untouched by it, that a shared tag refuses both mutations from the server rather than from what the client chose to render, and that deleting a personal tag leaves the shared library whole.

Someone writing a journal page -- including a Course reader writing a reflection, which is an ordinary page opened with a prefilled title -- taps the camera in the entry's top-right row (beside the key and the close X), photographs a page or screenshot of their response -- handwritten, typed, printed, or a screenshot of a message thread, which transcribes as sender-labelled lines -- and the transcription is appended into the entry they already had open rather than being filed as a second one. Overlapping screenshots of one thread merge without repeating the overlap: where two adjacent pages repeat lines at their seam (a cropped line at either edge included), the merged transcript carries them once, a quiet per-page notice counts the repeated lines by page position, and a "Keep them" action restores both copies for that seam; each page's stored text is never altered, a short or single coincidental repeat is never dropped, lines whose numbers, times, symbols or emoji differ never count as repeats, and a seam beside a hand-edited page is left whole so the writer's correction always reaches the entry (#2929). The seam is what makes that a single entry: the capture route hands the merged transcript back through an in-memory store and the open page's own create-then-update writer persists it, so the title and save context the writer arrived with survive and one POST /journal/ covers the whole journey. The outcome also includes a production deployment with no vision model configured: it refuses before billing with model_lacks_vision, shows the terminal copy and hand-typed-entry offramp, and keeps Save disabled (#2849); and an image with no text, or a read the model declines, which the server answers with an uncharged 422 no_text_found / transcription_refused that the page offers to Retake or Remove, never as its text (#2851). Uncovered because neither lane can drive the capture: the route auto-launches the device photo picker on mount, which the node lane cannot even mount (#2324) and which no browser spec has ever driven through a file chooser, and the transcription itself is a charged vision call that needs the lane's LLM stub wired through it.

A writer uses the same journal entry at 390x844, the 600px two-column boundary, and 1280x720, writing and then reading. Live browser boxes, each viewport read in one settled frame, prove every control keeps one home (#3002, #3004). While writing, the icon-only camera sits in the entry's top-right exit row directly left of the close X (same line, at least a 44px target, its full phrase only as the accessible name, and key, camera, X ahead of the title in DOM order), with no Edit beside it; neither the exit row nor the page scrolls sideways; under the body come the formatting toolbar, then the save footer, then Finish alone and centred under the body input. After the real autosave creates the entry and the writer pauses, Get Resonance is measured inside and centred on the wide marginalia column, its longest preflight state is held and measured within that fixed column, and at 600px and on the phone it is still the one Get Resonance on the page, inside the margin (stacked under the page on the phone) and in the page flow, never floating. Finishing turns the page to reading: at 390 and 1280 an icon-only Edit (accessible name 'Edit this entry') sits in the exit row directly left of the X on one line, at least 44px, with no camera and no Edit in the reading row; Promote sits below the save hint; resonance stays in the margin; nothing scrolls sideways. The journey then makes a real curriculum reflection due, opens it through the shelf invitation, writes a line so Finish appears, and at 600, 390 and 375px measures the reflection-only Sources as an icon in the exit row -- key, Sources, camera, X ahead of the title -- all on one line without sideways scroll, with neither Sources nor the camera on the rail and Finish still centred under the page, covering the widest writing row rather than inferring its geometry from component props.

Someone opens Past prompts from the journal shelf and reads the weekly questions they have already answered with what they wrote under each. Answering a prompt mirrors the response into the journal as an ordinary page, which keeps the writing and loses the question that drew it, so this route is the only one that returns the pair -- and nothing asked for it until this surface existed. What the seam has to prove is that a submitted response comes back joined to its own question, and that the limit and offset the modal sends actually slice the set rather than being ignored.

A person lets a habit rest during a Metta Return arc, then leaves the arc, and takes the habit up again from the Return surface -- no long-press on a locked tile, no 3-dot menu. The press is asserted on the server rather than on the card: the release row reads re-committed and the habit itself is unlocked again in the account's own habit list, which is the collection read that reconciles auto-reveals, so the pause is shown outranking the program's schedule while it holds and releasing it afterwards. That the row and not merely the habit recorded the re-commit is probed by locking the habit by hand from Habit Settings, which is the only thing that can tell the two halves of the reported flag apart. It runs in the browser lane because the journey is the card: the recovery affordance renders only on a shelf whose arc has ended while a release is outstanding, and the API lane cannot mount a React Native screen at all, so a spec there could only POST the route by hand. Deliberately under-claimed: only the recovery is pressed. Beginning the Return is its own journey (return.begin-a-return-from-the-journal-entry), and the let-go card that releases habits renders only in the session that started the arc, so release-then-leave is arranged over the same live wire -- every step read back, and Orange-stage eligibility asserted false before and true after the tests.e2e.program_anchor rewind, so an arrange that did nothing fails where it happened instead of leaving the press to test an empty shelf. The cross-tenant arm presses the same route from a second account holding an arc of its own: somebody else's habit id reads exactly like a nonexistent one, and the owner's own press afterwards proves that refusal is a refusal rather than a route that moves nothing. Verified to be a live gate: with recommit resolving the active arc again, as it did before the arc-spanning fix, the press 404s and the spec fails.

A journal entry whose resonance pass offers the Return is the card a person can begin one from: "Begin the Return" opens a confirmation naming the arc's five weekly foci as the server sent them, confirming opens an arc that lands on week one, and "Not now" persists the same decline the Journal shelf's offer card writes, so declining in the entry is honoured there. It runs in the browser lane because the journey is the card: the offer surfaces only while a resonance pass has just raised the in-memory contraction signal (src/store/useContractionSignalStore.ts) that useMettaReturn reads, and that store is fed by the screen's own pass -- the API lane cannot mount a screen at all, so a spec there could only call the two routes by hand. Both preconditions are arranged honestly: the contraction over the wire, from a habit whose foundation has been quiet past the detection window, and the Orange-stage eligibility by rewinding program_started_at through tests.e2e.program_anchor (no request schema accepts it) and then reading GET /stages, which is what records the entry -- eligibility is asserted false before and true after, so an arrange that did nothing fails rather than silently testing the simple_ease_off card. The double-tap latch is the one arm left to the Jest spec beside the component (src/features/Journal/__tests__/ContractionReflectionNote.test.tsx), which drives it deterministically; a browser cannot dispatch the second press without racing the first request. Verified to be a live gate: with confirmStart no longer calling start(), the spec fails on the arc POST that never leaves the browser.

A person whose reflections are still drawn from their last few entries is told so, in the sentence that is true for their own account: the consent decision if they have not made it -- with what saying yes gives, in the same words Settings uses (#3003) -- the import surface if they have and a vault is attached or unknown, or -- since #3017, for an account the server says has nothing attached -- Where your corpus lives, under the call to action 'Give your corpus a place to live'. The band is declinable in one tap, renders no count, and never blocks resonance. The lane drives the two states and the move between them across the wire on its own account.

A writer can set aside the one-time explanation of where reflections come from without losing the corpus door. A cold reload proves the dismissal persists; the Journal drawer then remains the corpus's sole Journal surface, beside the icon-bearing Photograph a page action, and a fresh undecided account reaches the actual consent screen through a live GET /corpus/voice-readiness decision. The two mounted drawer hosts and the gathering arms -- to the import surface with a vault attached or unknown, and to Where your corpus lives with nothing attached (#3017) -- are pinned in the adjacent component suites because the browser starts from only one readiness state. Retrying a failed 'Load older entries' in the same drawer asks again for the missing page and keeps the entries already shown (#2997); pinned in JournalDrawer.test.tsx because the e2e lane cannot force a mid-list failure. The same spec holds the drawer's door and every icon around it to the web's accessibility tree (#3009, #2829): with the console watched from the first page, the anonymous /get-started and /login pages (negative controls), the signed-in Journal shelf, the opened Journal drawer, the feedback composer and a new journal page each carry no React Native-only accessibility prop (accessible, accessibilityElementsHidden, importantForAccessibility) as a DOM attribute; the drawer toggle's svg, the Send feedback icon and the page's close X are aria-hidden="true"; and React logs no non-boolean-attribute or unknown-prop complaint about any of them. The one spelling behind it, decorativeHidden(), and the source guard that holds every file to it are pinned in Jest (a11yHidden.test.ts, decorativeHiddenGuard.test.ts).

A person sets a length on the journal's writing timer, writes until it runs out, is offered the session as a habit, and chooses where it sits among the habits they already signed up for — first position by default, with every other habit moving along one stage. The spec drives that write on its own account: it creates the habits the writer already had, then makes the placement the offer makes — one POST for the new habit carrying its stage and its place, one PUT per displaced row carrying theirs — and reads the list back. What only a live server can answer is whether the placement survives: that PUT /habits/{habit_id} keeps sort_order and stage instead of replacing them with the schema defaults, and that GET /habits/ then returns the rows in the order those numbers name, which is what makes the arrangement outlive a cold rehydrate. It also settles the lock: the row is created revealed=false like every other new habit, and the server's own one-shot reconciliation then opens it because Beige is a stage the writer has already reached — the spec pins both halves, and a habit at a stage they have not reached stays locked in the same pass. The offer's own rules (one-tap decline, a decline never re-asked, the stage preview) are pinned by the Jest specs beside WritingSessionOffer, and the offer's reachability from the writing page by JournalEntryScreenTimer.test.tsx; neither can cross the wire. What this spec cannot drive is the half-failure, because no live lane can refuse ONE displacing PUT in the middle of a fan-out: a POST that lands followed by a PUT that does not used to roll back the store alone, leaving a habit on the server the writer never confirmed under copy saying their habits were as they were. That branch is pinned beside habitManager instead (habitManager.test.ts: the created row is taken back off by the id its own POST returned; the branch where that DELETE is itself refused says the habit was saved out of place rather than reassuring; and a confirming re-fetch that fails after every write landed is not reported as a failed write).

A person finishes a timed writing session and is offered — beside the habit offer, under the same single decline — to keep it as the Journaling practice at Green. The offer describes what keeping it would do BEFORE it writes anything, because two things it would do are invisible from the journal page: Green may already hold a practice the writer chose (the server resolves a second open selection by closing the first, so a bare write evicts it silently), and Green may not be open to them yet (the selection is allowed as forward planning, but the just-finished session cannot be logged against it). This spec drives the server half on its own account, from a fresh signup standing at Beige — the harder half. It reads the seeded catalogue at stage 6 and pins that Journaling is there, approved, count_up, and twenty minutes; selects it at Green from Beige and pins that the server ACCEPTS the forward-planned pick, which is what makes the flow possible at all given that a mismatched stage_number is refused; pins that POST /practice-sessions/ against it is 403 stage_locked, which is why the client declines to send one and says so instead; reads the selection back by the effective_name the offer shows; and then puts another practice at Green and pins that the first row is CLOSED rather than the write refused — the silent eviction the offer names before the tap. The offer's own rules (one-tap decline, a decline never re-asked, the sentence shown before the write, no session claimed that was not logged) are pinned by the Jest specs beside WritingSessionOffer and SaveAsPracticeStep; none of them can cross the wire.

A writer finishes a timed writing session and is offered to keep it as a habit; the offer now asks which habit first, listing the ones they already keep by their own names with a new Journaling habit last. Choosing an existing one links the writing timer to it on the server (PATCH /ui-flags writing_session_habit_id), and from then on every finished session checks that habit off. The covering Playwright spec installs the browser clock before the app loads so a twenty-minute session can be run out in one step, signs up through the UI, seeds a habit, runs a first session and picks that habit from the picker, then reads GET /ui-flags back out of band to prove the link landed on the server. It runs a second session and waits for the POST /goal_completions/ that the habit pipeline sends, then reads GET /habits/{habit_id} back and pins the day's total at exactly the LOW tier target: 'checked off' means the low target is met today, and the amount posted is the gap to it, because since #2852 explicit amounts accumulate on the server and posting the session's minutes would push the habit further every time. A third session the same day posts nothing at all, which is the idempotency only the client's gap rule can supply. Deleting the habit then leaves GET /ui-flags unlinked. The cross-tenant refusal (403 with an audit row, and nothing written) is pinned in backend/tests/security/test_idor.py; the picker's rules, the offer's suppression once a link exists, the Settings row and the offer-again control are pinned by the Jest specs beside WritingSessionOffer, WritingHabitPicker and JournalSection.

A writer whose writing timer has no habit linked finishes a full-length session and the note it leaves points to Settings, where one can be chosen (#3006). On an ordinary page the keep-this offer has the first note to itself -- one invitation per note -- so declining it adds nothing to that note; the next finished session, with the offer answered and GET /ui-flags still unlinked, carries the link-a-habit note with two actions, Go to Settings and Don't show again. Go to Settings opens Settings with focus writing-habit: the Journal group's writing-habit row is scrolled into view with the WritingHabitPicker already open under it, and choosing the writer's habit there PATCHes /ui-flags (read back out of band). Back on the page, the next finished session checks that habit off and carries no note. The covering Playwright spec drives all of that with the browser clock. Jest pins the rest: LinkHabitNudge.test.tsx (nothing while the link is unknown or the flag read is pending, the server link winning over an unset flag, Don't show again hiding at once and persisting), JournalEntryScreenTimer.test.tsx (the note on a quick-launched page, which never makes the offer; the arbitration on an ordinary page; a later page after Don't show again), linkHabitNudgeStorage.test.ts (fail-open read, a save that never rejects, a restore that resolves whether it saved), and JournalSection.test.tsx plus SettingsHubScreen.test.tsx (the focus opening the picker and scrolling, and the Show the habit note again row saying it is back only when the restore saved).

A user who already has habits reopens the scaffolding modal from the drawer or the energy footer and re-runs it. A habit they enter again keeps its own row: the new energy rating, icon, stage and staggered start date are PUT onto the id the server issued, while the streak, the check-ins, the goal ids and the unlock flag survive untouched. Before this, that pick was POSTed, the server rejected the duplicate name with a 409, the client swallowed it into a console line, and the rating the user had just confirmed was silently discarded while the stale row kept its old one -- only a habit under a genuinely new name ever appeared. A habit carried along from before the program is matched too, and stays on the negative lap with its own beginning rather than being scaffolded onto a program date. A habit the picks do not mention is retained, never released: the delete cascades that habit's goals and completions server-side and cannot be undone, so it follows only an explicit choice. That explicit release is implemented and unit-tested here -- deletes are awaited before any create, so a released name can be re-entered without the create hitting the same unique index -- and the review step now gives the user a way to state one, behind a confirmation that names the habit and says its check-ins and goals go with it. Uncovered because the seam runs through the habit service rather than the API client the lane drives directly: reaching it needs a lane that can open the modal, which is what the linked issue tracks. Pinned meanwhile by the "onboardingSave merge" block in src/features/Habits/services/__tests__/habitManager.test.ts, which drives the merge through the same bare picks the screen passes and asserts the exact create/update/delete call counts, the phase ordering, and that no fabricated id reaches the wire.

A person finishes a timed writing session, is offered that session as a habit inside the note the page leaves them, then starts a second session and abandons it partway. The offer is still there afterwards, still holding whatever they had chosen, and accepting it still saves the habit on their own account. That is the lifetime the note's children slot promises: an offer goes away only when the writer closes the note, or when a later session runs its full length and replaces the note with one about that newer session — never because a session was merely started, paused, or stopped early. The slot now holds a real offer, and both halves of the rule are pinned by the Jest specs beside WritingSessionSurface (WritingSessionOfferSlot.test.tsx: a standing offer survives an abandoned session, and is rebuilt when a newer session replaces the note). Still uncovered across the wire because the claim is about a mounted component surviving an interaction, and this lane runs on the node environment with node_modules untransformed and cannot mount a screen at all — the constraint #2324 records. The write the offer performs is covered end to end by journal.timed-writing-session-becomes-a-habit; what is missing is a rendering lane that can drive the surviving offer to it.

A user who already has habits opens Energy Scaffolding and is asked about them before anything else. Every habit they own is listed with a tick, ticked; for each ticked one they choose Bring along -- already mastered, tracked on the carryover pages -- or Re-rate, which puts it back in the pool to be rated and slotted into the new energy order with its stored ratings already on the sliders. Unticking one is how a habit is let go of, and it is the only irreversible thing on the step: continuing then names the habits by name and says their check-ins and goals go with them, and cancelling leaves every tick exactly where it was. Brought-along habits never reach the energy, reveal, reorder or template steps and never count against the ten-habit ceiling, so a user with ten habits who brings four along can still add four. Before this the modal opened on a blank page and whatever the user typed was appended beside everything they already had. Uncovered for the same reason as welcome.first-run-walkthrough-to-journal and habits.scaffolding-start-date-anchors-the-program: this lane runs on the node environment with node_modules untransformed and cannot mount a screen at all, and every step of this journey is inside a modal. Pinned meanwhile by src/features/Habits/components/__tests__/OnboardingModal.reviewStep.test.tsx, which drives the whole flow through the rendered modal to the plan the save receives, and by src/features/Habits/components/__tests__/onboardingReview.test.ts for the decisions themselves.

A user whose habits were created before sort_order existed holds NULL in every row. GET /habits/ used to order by sort_order ASC with no NULLS placement and no secondary key, so the order among those rows was undefined and PostgreSQL sorted them last -- the first numbered habit the user added leapfrogged every habit they had onboarded with, and because tile colour is positional (HabitsScreen colorIndices) the whole lap repainted around it. The list query now orders by sort_order ASC NULLS FIRST, then id: the unnumbered rows keep the head position they have always displayed in, a later numbered add lands after them, and the id key makes the order total even for a fully numbered store, where two rows may legitimately share a slot because slots restart at zero inside each is_carryover partition. Uncovered because the e2e lane cannot mint a pre-2026-09-02 store: the production client always stamps a slot on the rows it creates, so reaching the NULL population needs a fixture the lane has no seam for. Pinned meanwhile by backend/tests/test_habits_list_ordering.py, which asserts the ORDER BY the endpoint actually emitted, compiled to the PostgreSQL dialect -- the test lane is SQLite, which sorts NULLs first natively and cannot tell the fix from the defect.

A person deletes a habit they have actually used, and it stays deleted. The order is the finding: a habit created moments ago always deleted cleanly, and one that had ever been checked in returned 500, so this journey checks in on the clear goal, confirms the completion is really on the wire, and only then asks for the delete. The backend suite could not see this at all -- it runs on SQLite built from the model metadata, which until #2763 was not enforcing foreign keys, so a cascade that never ran and a cascade that ran perfectly left the same green. Here the schema is the migrated Postgres one and the four ON DELETE CASCADE constraints are the real ones. The re-read after the delete is what the reporter's next screen did: the symptom was a tile that came back, because the client reverts its optimistic removal when the server rejects.

Someone connects a private vault of their own from Settings (Your corpus, then Where your corpus lives, then the Advanced: connect a vault you run yourself section, which is closed until they open it): the screen reads whether one is attached, they paste an address and a key, the server refuses an address it cannot reach securely and writes no row for it, and a good one comes back connected with no credential on the reply. Both halves are green on their own — the screen's tests mock the client and the router's tests never build a request — so this is the one place they agree on the paths, the verbs, the refusal codes and the write-only credential. It pins four refusals rather than one -- an insecure transport, a destination only a local network can reach, an address that resolves nowhere, and a key no Authorization header could carry -- because the server judges where a URL points as well as how it is shaped, and the screen answers each with its own sentence.

Someone with a vault attached presses Disconnect, or presses Connect with a different address or key (or while the read failed). The card and the form live behind the Advanced section, which opens on first render when a vault of their own is connected, so Disconnect needs no press to find; after a read that failed it stays closed until opened. Either press opens a rendered confirmation, not Alert.alert, which react-native-web ships as an empty method (#2928). Confirming sends DELETE or PUT /vault/connection exactly once; cancelling sends nothing. Only Disconnect is styled destructive. Generic PUT/DELETE now refuse with 409 when this account has a managed binding or an activation whose teardown is not confirmed; neither confirmation abandons a managed allocation (#3049). Backend API regressions cover lifecycle states and handoff during URL validation. The interim UI proof is src/features/Settings/__tests__/VaultSettingsScreen.test.tsx; a browser proof needs a VaultSettings web path and a routable vault fake.

Someone opens Where your corpus lives from the Your corpus group in Settings and finds the bring-your-own form folded behind 'Advanced: connect a vault you run yourself' (#3007). The fold says what it is, who it is for and what it is not, links the plain-language guide in docs/your-data.md, and is closed by default -- open on first render only when GET /vault/connection names a vault of their own, so Disconnect is never hidden. It is remembered for the visit only. A connected response with a hidden address is shown as a managed connection without claiming live health (#3050); failed reads remain unknown and managed replacement still requires confirmation. The managed offer and the read's notices sit outside it, and the feedback line sits after it, so a read that failed is still said while it is closed. The interim proof is src/features/Settings/__tests__/VaultSettingsScreen.test.tsx; a browser proof needs the same VaultSettings web path and routable vault fake as vault.disconnect-or-replace-confirmed.

An authenticated, server-eligible user chooses managed-vault activation from Settings after signup, sees on web, iOS, and Android that ordinary Fly custody is provider-managed/operator-readable, not confidential compute, and still excludes INTIMATE content, then explicitly starts an allocation. The production client crosses the live Adepthood API and Postgres lifecycle into an isolated fake Creek 2.0 control plane. The fake first returns a terminal provider rejection, Adepthood exposes the bounded recovery action, and the cleanup screen explains that secure deletion may take up to 24 hours, can be left and revisited, and does not block journaling. Creek confirms authenticated deletion, and only then does a fresh generation progress through pending and provisioning, receive the authenticated one-way connection handoff, and reach ready with an explicit provider_managed custody value. Unit journeys beside PrivateVaultActivationScreen pin the optional consent, unavailable/ineligible state, emergency-disable replay, truthful custody copy, absence of ceremony controls, cleanup retry behavior, and legacy wrapped-artifact wording; this seam spec pins every live route and schema between that screen and the two services.

A traveller reads a stage's subtitle -- the two-word label under its name -- on the Map modal, the Map's centre-cell accessibility label, the magnifier caption, and the Course cover. Every one of those renders stage.subtitle verbatim from GET /stages via stageService, and nothing is hardcoded client-side, which is exactly why the covering spec names no subtitle of its own: it reads the coursestage rows out of band, requires the served listing to match them stage for stage, then rewrites one row to a string the curriculum has never held and requires the client to follow it there -- an assertion that a route answering with its own copy of the seeded words cannot pass. What the server served is then fed through stageCenterCellLabel, the function MapScreen hands its centre cell, so the sentence a screen reader speaks is bound to the row too; the row is put back before the file ends. map.advance-stage opens the same screen against the same route but asserts the progress record (current_stage, completed_stages, stage_started_at) and never copy, so this journey keeps its own spec rather than widening that claim. #2577 corrected Teal's subtitle and was proven by a backend golden test, which pins the string at the source and says nothing about whether the client renders it.

A traveller reads a stage's free-will archetype -- the persona beside each stage in the Map's left column and in its spoken label -- and it is the course's own archetype as the coursestage row holds it: Purple reads Pleasure Seeker, the name its free-will chapter and the aptitude-stages.md heading use. Since #2666 nothing about it is hardcoded client-side: stageService fills the stage store from GET /stages and stageVocabulary.ts derives the persona from relationship_to_free_will, so the covering spec names no persona of its own. It reads the persona the Map shows, rewrites that stage's row out of band with tests.e2e.stage_copy set-field (which reports the value it replaced) and requires the replaced value to be exactly what was on screen, then reloads and requires the left column and the hotspot's aria-label to follow the row to a string the curriculum never held -- an assertion a client answering from its own copy of the seeded words cannot pass. The row is put back before the file ends. The Journal AspectChordControl reads the same persona without a program visit: from the stage store when the Map or Practice filled it, otherwise from GET /stages/correspondence, otherwise the stage colour name; that path is pinned by frontend/src/features/Journal/__tests__/useAspectOptions.test.tsx and JournalEntryScreenChord.test.tsx rather than a browser spec.

A writer who has asked for reflections before asks for another one, and the Higher Self does not say a thing it has already said: at most two of the letters it wrote them earlier ride along with the pass as content-only context, under a pinned instruction never to imitate their wording or treat them as a voice sample. A letter about an entry they deleted, or one they later marked Intimate, is never among them, and neither is a letter about the page being read. Uncovered for the same reason as journal.ask-for-resonance and journal.see-related-vault-pages: what changes here is generated prose rather than a screen or a new seam, and the real-wire lane has no deterministic language-model provider, so it cannot make POST /journal/{entry_id}/resonance return notes it could read back and compare across two passes. #2408 tracks that missing provider seam. The exclusions are pinned end-to-end at the endpoint by backend/tests/test_intimate_privacy_guard.py::test_only_eligible_prior_letters_reach_the_cloud_prompt, and the query that decides them by backend/tests/test_prior_letters_grounding.py.

A writer presses OK on a completion-suggestion card in the journal margin and the accept is refused. The refusal is named where the writer is looking -- beside the very card that produced it, not in place of it -- and announced through a polite live region rather than only drawn, while the card stays pending and pressable so a second press really does check the habit off. The spec drives that over the real wire in a real browser: only the literary pass is intercepted, to reach a suggestion card without an LLM, while detection, the row, the refused accept, the retry and the persisted acceptance are all the live server. A 500 stands in for the class the margin used to swallow -- a 401, a 404, a 409 on an already-dismissed row, a request that never arrives -- because every one reaches the same catch. What no browser spec can reach is pinned beside it in Jest: src/features/Journal/__tests__/useResonance.test.tsx holds the copy to what the client can actually observe (a blocked preflight and an unreachable host are one bare TypeError), pins the habit-store refresh to the auth-hydrated zone rather than the device's, and pins that a success retires only its own card's complaint -- with two cards on screen, accepting one must not erase the other's still-live failure while that card is still pending.

Someone whose library has outgrown one page reads it whole. The client pages every list endpoint at fifty rows a page (api/index.ts, listAll -> fetchAllPages), and paginate_query used to apply OFFSET/LIMIT to whatever the router handed it and add no ordering of its own -- so GET /user-practices/ carried no ORDER BY at all, and neighbouring endpoints ordered on keys that tie (a practice-session timestamp, a recipe owner-and-name, a stageprogress user_id). OFFSET/LIMIT is only well-defined over a total order: inside a tie group the database may order each page request differently, so one selection can arrive on two consecutive pages while another arrives on none, and the reader sees a duplicate or a hole with nothing wrong in the store. paginate_query now appends the entity primary key to every page it serves, which is a no-op wherever the caller key was already total. Uncovered because the seam is a page boundary: this lane cannot mint the fifty-one rows that produce a second page without a fixture seam it has no route for, and even with one, an assertion on returned rows cannot tell the fix from the defect -- a planner is free to return the tie group in insertion order either way. Pinned meanwhile by backend/tests/test_pagination_total_order.py, which asserts the ORDER BY each endpoint actually emitted, compiled to the PostgreSQL dialect the test lane is not.

Someone whose Journaling practice is saved taps one button in the Practice player and lands on a blank journal page with the practice's own length already running; when the page's session ends it is recorded against that selection, and the "keep this as a practice?" offer is not put to them again. Uncovered because the one claim this adds over journal.timed-writing-session-becomes-a-practice is the COMPLEMENT of what that spec pins: that spec deliberately stands its account at Beige and proves POST /practice-sessions/ answers 403 stage_locked against a forward-planned Journaling selection at Green, which is why the launch sends nothing there. What is unproven end-to-end is the same request SUCCEEDING once Green has actually opened -- and reaching that state needs backend/tests/e2e/program_anchor.py to move the account's program anchor five stages back and a read of GET /stages/program-calendar to make the record catch up, then its own spec file, its own account via freshLicenseKey(), and e2eLaneGuard registration. Pinned meanwhile on the client side by src/features/Practice/__tests__/PracticeScreenQuickLaunch.test.tsx (the button exists only for a saved Journaling practice, and navigates with the override-aware length and the selection id) and src/features/Journal/__tests__/useQuickLaunchedSession.test.tsx (the finished session is recorded once, for the length actually written, and never sent when the stage is still ahead) -- both of which agree with themselves about a server that is not there.

A writer on the Journal shelf sets a stage prompt aside, finds it gone from the band and still gone after a cold start on a new session, brings it back, and is never told they skipped or failed anything. The invariant this crosses the wire for is the one a mocked test cannot see: a dismissal is a preference and never a completion, so the spec sets a prompt aside and then still writes a response to another prompt in the same week, proving the set-aside wrote no PromptResponse, marked nothing answered, did not move the reader's week and did not close the week to the prompts still standing. It also pins that the weekly prompt drawn from the same curriculum carries the same answer, that a repeated set-aside collapses onto the unique index rather than adding a second row, that undoing one that was never made is success, that an ordinal the stage does not carry and a stage the reader has not reached are refused exactly as the stage read refuses them, and -- the half a mis-scoped WHERE would make indistinguishable -- that one account's un-set-aside never removes another's, the prompt being named by curriculum position which is identical for everyone.

A practitioner opens Practice on a session whose one automatic GET /stages did not come back, and is told so instead of being shown stage 1 as though it were theirs. Practice takes a single stage-load attempt per session (#2002), and when it fails the store still holds its initial currentStage of 1 -- so the screen used to render that number silently, with the only in-app recovery being a trip to Map's retry. The spec fails the real listing at the wire, crosses to Practice through the drawer, and pins the three claims together: the number is named as a placeholder, the adopted practice underneath it is still on screen and still startable (this is a notice, not an error wall -- a person who only wants to sit is never gated), and lifting the failure and tapping Try again adds exactly ONE more request to the route and takes the notice away in the same page load. That last count is the half no mocked suite can make: it is the guard from #2002 -- automatic attempts stay at one, the retry is the deliberate second -- measured against a real server rather than against a stub that agrees with itself.

A user completes a habit, leaves the app open across their local midnight, and looks again: the habit reads as not-yet-done today, its tier stars return to unlit, and the journal shelf's "Today's habits" count is back to zero -- with nothing remounted and no completion rewritten. Returning to the Habits tab or the shelf also re-reads habits from the server rather than showing whatever the store held when the tab was first opened, and so does foregrounding the app onto the tab the user never left -- the half #2764's acceptance criteria missed, since navigation reports no focus for a screen that never lost it (#2847). The covering Playwright spec pins the browser to Los Angeles, checks in a revealed habit's stretch tier over POST /goal_completions/, and installs the page clock on the day the server recorded that completion. On a Habits screen at 23:58 the tile reads ACHIEVED TODAY! with met tier stars; three minutes later, on the same page with no reload, it reads neither. The midnight boundary is not purely client-side any more: since #2847 it re-reads GET /habits/ on the focused screen, and the spec answers exactly that one read 404 (not retried, not applied), so the turnover comes from the client re-deriving today from rows it already held rather than from fresh server data. No POST /goal_completions/ crosses the boundary and GET /habits/{id} still carries the original completion on its original local_day. The shelf reads 1/1 done before midnight and 0/1 after while mounted, and each drawer hop costs exactly one paginated GET /habits/: one on arriving at Habits (the arrival is not double-fetched), one on returning to the shelf, one on returning to Habits. A hidden-then-visible visibilitychange -- what react-native-web's AppState reports as background and active -- re-reads the never-left tab exactly once. What the browser cannot isolate is either surface's own day subscription: the boundary read toggles the store's loading slice, which re-renders the shelf and makes the Habits screen swap its grid for a spinner, so the tiles mount afresh whether or not they listen to the day. Both subscriptions stay pinned in Jest (HabitTileDayRollover, useHabitsSummary and ResumedSessionDayBoundary). The resumed-session half is registered separately as habits.resumed-session-reads-its-own-calendar.

A user west of UTC whose device holds a session token but no cached zone -- one that signed in before #2847 cached it -- opens the app after 17:00 local, when UTC has turned over and their day has not. The resumed session should carry the zone the server has on record, fetched by one POST /auth/refresh, so yesterday evening's completion still reads as today rather than running on the UTC default. That is the bug as reported: "I just had to log out and log back in to get my habits to reset for today." Uncovered because driving it through the browser lane exposes a defect on the same path (#3034): the backfill's refresh rotates the token, revoking the one the app's first wave of requests is still carrying; those requests come back 401, the 401 handler refreshes whichever token the session holds at that instant, and either that refresh revokes the token the first one just minted (a cascade of refreshes that only succeeds because the lane disarms the 1/minute limiter) or it presents the already-revoked resumed token and the session is signed out to the get-started screen. Pinned in process meanwhile by src/context/__tests__/ResumedSessionDayBoundary.test.tsx, which joins the real AuthProvider to the real useHabitsSummary at 08:00 in Los Angeles.

A writer opens the shelf of letters their margin notes grew into. GET /journal/voice-drafts shipped in #2606 with no client, no screen and no call site at all, so the route was served and unreachable; this is the PR that makes the crossing exist and therefore the PR that declares it. The spec drives the shelf the way the screen does: a fresh account's shelf answers 200 with an empty page (the first-run state the screen renders is built on that, not on an error), a margin note is generated and then heard out at length through the real resonance and essay routes, and the expansion those routes wrote turns up on the listing carrying its whole letter, its anchor text and its parent entry id -- which is what lets the screen open a draft with no second request and walk back to the page it was written in the margin of. The window the client asks for is exercised past the end of the shelf, where an empty page with has_more false is what retires the screen's Older letters row. A cold login sees the same shelf, an unauthenticated read is refused 401, and a neighbouring account gets an empty shelf rather than a stranger's prose. The expansion is generated rather than fixtured on purpose: the listing selects exactly the rows the essay path writes, so a fixture would prove the listing reads a table rather than that the two routes agree about what an expanded note is. What no spec here asserts is the product stance -- no badge, no count, no nudge -- because that is a claim about what the screen does NOT render; it is pinned in VoiceDraftsShelfScreen.test.tsx and JournalDrawer.test.tsx instead, where the rendered tree can be read. Retrying a failed Older letters read asks again for the missing page and keeps the letters already shown (#2902); that is pinned in VoiceDraftsShelfScreen.test.tsx too, because the e2e lane cannot force a mid-shelf failure.

A private-beta tester opens the feedback composer from the Send feedback control in the app shell's header (present on Journal, Habits, Practice, Course and Map) or from the Settings hub, chooses what kind of report it is, answers that kind's questions, sees exactly which of the seven allowlisted context fields will be attached, and sends it under one idempotency key minted and persisted with the draft. The live intake route answers with a public reference such as FB-7K3M9Q2B, which the composer shows only after feedbackReceiptSchema has validated it, and which resolves through GET /feedback/{public_id}/receipt to the tester's own receipt. The covering Playwright spec drives the whole path keyboard-only at 1280x720 -- Tab to the header control, focus lands on the composer heading, focus returns to the control on close -- and again at 390x844, and measures the header control against the drawer toggles, the Journal new-page action, the Habits first-use action and the Map magnifier. The same spec runs an origin matrix -- all five tabs and Settings at 1280x720, Journal and Map again at 390x844 -- asserting the screen, control and viewport class each attaches; files a compact report from a Journal whose shelf load was made to fail, double-clicked, and proves exactly one POST left the page and that its context equals the rendered preview key for key; and files a keyboard-only confusing report from the wide Map. Lost responses, a reload mid-send, offline, 422 and 429 are provoked deterministically with Playwright routing in feedback.recover-a-lost-send; a receipt that fails validation stays pinned in FeedbackComposer.test.tsx. The lane's server disarms the rate limiter, so the server's own 429 is pinned in process by backend/tests/test_rate_limits.py; the backend suites pin the 422 on an eighth context key, the one-row concurrency guarantee under a shared Idempotency-Key (on real PostgreSQL in backend/tests/integration/test_feedback_intake_race.py), the closed screen and control vocabularies that refuse prose dressed as a token, and the byte-identical cross-tenant 404.

An operator, confirmed by GET /admin/capabilities rather than by anything the client infers, opens the Beta feedback inbox from Settings, reads a report, moves it along the triage table, adds a private note, and prepares an issue draft. What the covering spec proves is the seam: it drives the unmocked production client against a live server -- a reporter files a report, a second account is promoted in the lane database (is_admin has no HTTP writer), the reporter files the two reports the browser journeys file (a compact-Journal broken report and a wide-Map confusing one, filed through the client because the browser lane has its own database), the reporter and a bystander are both refused every operator question including the transition and note actions, the bystander gets the byte-identical 404 on the reporter's receipt, and neither refusal moves status, notes or events. The operator lists both reports and sees reporter_said, app_attached and operator_added kept apart for each; the draft carries the envelope evidence on labelled lines and none of the reporter's address, correlation id or words. Finally the reporter's export carries both reports, and after the account is deleted the operator can neither open nor list them. It renders no screen. The UI half is proven in Jest instead, not across the seam: SettingsHubScreen.test (the row appears only on a 200 from capabilities and navigates to AdminFeedback), navigation/__tests__/RootStack.test (the route is registered), and the AdminFeedback screen, flow and draft-panel tests.

A tester's report survives the network failing at each point a real send can fail, in a real browser against the live intake route. Playwright routing makes each failure deterministic: the response is lost after the server committed (route.fetch then route.abort, for every automatic retry too), and Send again returns the very reference the server stored; the page is reloaded while the POST is still held, and the composer reopens on the frozen draft with Send again, sends nothing by itself, and one press files one report under the key minted before the reload; the browser goes offline, the draft stays frozen, and back online one resend files one report; a 422 and a 429 answered in the server's place show the composer's own copy, the 422 unfreezes the draft, the 429 is retried a bounded number of times under the same key, and the server holds no report. Every resend in every journey carries one Idempotency-Key, and the report count is read from the account's own export. The lane's server runs with the rate limiter disarmed, so a server-side 429 is not provoked here; the intake limits stay pinned in process by backend/tests/test_rate_limits.py.

A tester who has just hit a failure -- the Journal shelf failing to load, say -- reports it from a control on the error state itself, and the report carries a stable error code naming the failure as context.control. Uncovered because the entry point does not exist yet: #2898 AC24 was deferred, so the only controls that open the composer are the shell header and the Settings row, and a report filed after a failure carries the header token (feedback-composer.browser.e2e.test.ts files exactly that). Adding it means adding each code to the closed FeedbackControl vocabulary on both sides, not widening the check.

Someone using a screen reader opens a screen whose stack header already shows its title -- Settings, Support & care, Voice drafts, Promoted quotes, the beta feedback inbox, Time zone, Export my data, Delete account, Where your corpus lives (the vault screen, #3007) or managed-vault activation -- and hears that title as a heading exactly once (#2962): the stack header is the screen's one heading, and the body paints no second title and adds no second header named by it, visible or not. The covering Playwright spec signs up through the UI and opens each of the ten screens at 390x844 and 1280x720 -- eight the way the text census reaches them, Promoted quotes through the Journal drawer, and the operator inbox through its Settings row -- and counts the elements with role heading whose accessible name is the title, which must be one. Managed-vault activation used to paint a paraphrase of its title (#2995), so there the spec also counts the headings inside the screen body, which must be none. A lane account is never an operator, so the one GET /admin/capabilities answer that shows the inbox row is fulfilled in the browser; the inbox paints the same header either way, and nothing else is stubbed.

Every screen's text is in order: each string sits inside the component it describes, groups share one edge, a region uses few faces, and no raw Markdown reaches the screen (epic #2946; the reviewer's protocol is prompts/scans/text-order.md, landed by #2947). The covering Playwright spec signs up through the UI, seeds ten habits, one adopted practice with a share link and one journal entry over the API, then walks every reachable route -- the five tabs (Journal, Habits, Practice, Course, Map) and every RootStack screen a lane account can open -- at 390x844 and 1280x720, screenshots each and reduces it to a census of every visible text node (string, face, size, weight, colour, box, nearest testID) written under e2e/artifacts/text-order/ and published by CI as text-order-census. Three rules are asserted mechanically per screen because geometry can hold them: (A) no text box leaves its closest testID ancestor by more than a pixel, measured against the ancestor's scroll extent when it scrolls; (B) no two unrelated text boxes overlap by more than a pixel, nested Text spans excluded; (C) no visible string carries **, __, ## or [text](. Off-ramp font sizes -- sizes outside the set computed from type(width), editorialType and uiType, which a Jest bridge pins to the tokens -- are reported per screen and written to the JSON, and asserted empty only on a route whose remediation issue has landed (OFF_RAMP_ASSERTED): the Map since #2960, the Practice player, catalog and details since #2963, API key, Timezone, Export data, Delete account, managed-vault activation and the shared-practice preview since #2962, and the Course landing since #2964, at both viewports. Everywhere else they are deliberately not asserted -- hundreds of fontSize literals outside the tokens would red the lane -- and promoting a route's column to a gate is the exit criterion of its per-screen remediation issue. Everything that needs judgement -- one edge, one face per role, scope, glyph over word, eyebrows -- is printed as the per-screen summary line (distinct left edges, distinct faces) and is a review step per the protocol, not an assertion. AdminFeedback (admin gate), JournalPhotograph (no camera in headless Chromium; a read page would be a paid transcription), Get resonance and voice transcription are named in SKIPPED and logged on every run; nothing the walk does spends.

Every screen's controls are in order: the Action rows rules in frontend/src/design/DESIGN.md (#2860) -- (a) a card's one decline is the top-right X, (b) confirm and decline share one right-aligned row with the decline tertiary, (c) a form's primary action is full-width or centred at the bottom, (d) no lone text link under a card on its own line, (e) sibling controls share one baseline and one edge. The covering Playwright spec signs up through the UI, seeds the same account as the text census (ten habits, one adopted practice with a share link, one journal entry) over the API, then walks every route e2e/routeWalk.ts reaches plus Promoted quotes at 390x844 and 1280x720. A band that fetches its own state after mount is waited for before its screen is measured, so it is held to the rules every run rather than on the runs it wins the race: the Journal shelf's voice-readiness band is served a not-yet-consented readiness (the real GET /corpus/voice-readiness response with its body pinned) and the shelf is measured only once the band and its corner X are both visible. For each screen it reads every visible accessibilityRole=button box in ONE settled frame (two requestAnimationFrames inside one evaluate), prints one line per button (viewport, screen, testID, box, name), and writes e2e/artifacts/action-rows/<viewport>/<route>.{png,json}, which CI publishes as action-row-sweep with if: always(). Three consequences of the rules are asserted because geometry can hold them: no two unrelated buttons overlap by more than a pixel, no button leaves the viewport's width (a sideways-scrolling rail excepted), and buttons side by side -- each one's vertical centre inside the other's extent -- have tops within 2px. A deliberately broken fixture page proves the walker catches each violation, and an inventory test, read from RootStackParamList and RootTabParamList, fails any screen neither walked nor skipped and any button skip on a route the walk never opens. Buttons in one scroller are compared in its content coordinates, so rows below the fold are held to the rules too; buttons in different scroll containers are compared where both are on screen. AdminFeedback (admin gate) and JournalPhotograph (no camera; a read page would be a paid transcription) are skipped with reasons logged every run, as is one button: the Map's draggable magnifier lens, which parks over the current stage's own hotspots by design and is left to the review step while every other Map control is held to the rules; a skipped button whose control has left its screen fails the sweep. Rules (a) to (e) themselves are a review step over the screenshots, not assertions; nothing the walk does spends.

Someone opens a stage deep link -- /practice/1 or /course/1, typed, bookmarked or tapped from outside the app -- and lands on that stage. React Navigation hands a path segment to the screen as a string while the screens compare stage numbers strictly, so before #2958 the linking config's missing parse step made /practice/1 show 'No practice set for this stage yet.' to an account whose adopted practice is stage 1 (the #2948 census finding), and made /course/1 render with no stage cover, no metadata and no stage chip selected. The spec seeds a fresh account's stage-1 adoption over the API, loads /practice/1 and asserts the adopted practice's name and Begin control with no empty state, then loads /course/1 (the course half: GET /course/stages/{stage_number}/content) and asserts the stage cover, the stage metadata and stage-pill-1 carrying the accent border (stagePillActive) while stage-pill-2 stays transparent -- react-native-web emits no aria-selected for the pill, so the spec reads the computed border colour. Only the browser takes the URL from the address bar through the web linking layer to the screen and on to a real server.
